item.title: Falcons vs. Saints odds: Opening lines for Week 4 matchup
item.description: Atlanta heads down to New Orleans for a rivalry matchup on Monday Night Football, with the Falcons taking on the Saints in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Things are looking very different for the Falcons heading into their second consecutive primetime game in Week 4. After an 0-2 start with reserve quarterback Cooper Rush at the helm, Atlanta finally got their starting quarterback into the lineup in Week 3. Michael Penix Jr. provided the spark the team desperately needed on offense, and the Falcons came away with a dominant upset victory over the Packers.

Now Atlanta heads down to New Orleans for a rivalry matchup on Monday Night Football. The Saints are also coming into this game at 1-2 after a multitude of fourth quarter turnovers cost them the game against the Las Vegas Raiders. Monday’s game could hand the winner the early lead in the beleaguered NFC South, so how do the oddsmakers view the matchup?

The Saints opened as 2.5-point home favorites per FanDuel—a line that would’ve shocked many just a week ago, given the Falcons play the first two weeks. The moneyline for Monday Night Football is at -152 for New Orleans and +128 for Atlanta, and the over under is set at 48.5.

The Falcons haven’t quite earned our trust, although Week 3 was certainly a step in the right direction. Atlanta has an opportunity to put the first two weeks of the season firmly the in the rearview mirror with a victory over their hated rivals. The Saints are clearly vulnerable as one of the most turnover-prone offenses in the NFL, and the loss of left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. and running back Travis Etienne Jr. could be significant. This is Atlanta’s chance to get back to 2-2 and take control of a floundering NFC South. I just hope they actually take advantage, for once.

item.title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Won vs. the Philadelphia Eagles
item.description: Of course the Bears won Monday night with their third QB starting the game. Right? @BryanOrenchuk shares his three reasons Chicago defied the odds.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to the third installment of my new series for the 2026 season, where I recap what I believe were the three reasons the Chicago Bears won or lost the previous game.

In week 3, the Bears hosted the 2-0 Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night in front of a national audience and played inspired team football without Caleb Williams as he recovers from a hamstring injury. Here are my three reasons why they won.

1. Ben Johnson, HC

With the exception of one series where I would have liked for him to kick a field goal after Rome Odunze committed his weekly drop, this time in the endzone, Ben called his best game of the season and completely outcoached Nick Sirianni AND Eagles DC Vic Fangio. The fact that he did so with 3rd string QB Case Keenum (more on him later) was even more impressive. For me, I was most pleased with the decrease in penalties as that has been hindering us the first two weeks of the season. Ben had these Bears ready to play and bounce back from a lackluster effort the week prior in their first real emotional and mental test of the season. He also seemed to relish the opportunity to do so without a 1st overall pick at QB for him for the first time in his play calling career. Overall, it was a near 50/50 split of run and pass with some of the creative genius sprinkled throughout the game and the players were ready to play. I gave him blame last week in Chicago’s loss, and he bounced back in a big way against a playoff contender. Exactly what you like to see from your head coach.

2. Dennis Allen, DC

Speaking of coaches, Ben wasn’t the only one on Chicago’s sideline that was “in his bag” on Monday night. Don’t look now, but the former New Orleans Saints head coach has led this defense to two consecutive games holding Chicago opponents under 10 points per game. This week he did it with two rookies in the secondary against a Super Bowl winning team led by Super Bowl LIX MVP Jalen Hurts. Reminiscent of a vintage Lovie Smith performance, this defense played “bend but don’t break” ball all night. Though All-World RB Saquon Barkley ran for 5.5 yards per carry and consistently got the Eagles down the field, this Bears defense held the Eagles to only 7 points when they had scored 24 in each of their first two games of the season.

Allen consistently seemed to befuddle Hurts with the appearance of pressure only to bring it from elsewhere or drop back into coverage. Massive hat tip to Secondary Coach Al Harris for having those two rookies ready to play as well. This team is not the same without Harris coaching the DBs, and he and Allen are doing impressive things with that group that is, without arguably its best player in Safety Coby Bryant. Don’t look now, but these Bears are for real. Even on defense.

3. Case Keenum, QB

Nobody can possibly talk about this game without bringing up the performance and effort by 12 year vet Case Keenum who made his first start in over 1,000 days. Not only did Case “rush” for his first TD since 2019, but he threw for two more scores and displayed exceptional awareness all night – knowing when and where to go with the football and spreading the ball around to his playmakers. All in all, seven Bears caught passes from the 38 year old girl-dad who earned himself a game ball and post-game interview on ESPN with his daughter in his lap.

Is his arm strength near elite? No, it is not, but it’s hard to argue with the results after his pinpoint accuracy and consistently elite decision-making picked apart Fangio’s defense, which has arguably the most talented defensive roster in the league. It would be easy to forget that Case has been the QB3 this entire season and off-season. Meaning, this was the first and only week that he had any work in practice with the top weapons on the team. That matters from a timing and precision standpoint, but Case trusted in his supporting cast, and they rewarded him with an unforgettable win on Monday night. Things you love to see. Take a look at some of these moments captured by Film Watchers below. These things simply don’t happen without complete trust and awareness in the game plan. In my opinion, there is no way you start anyone else next game.

What about you? Who or what caught your attention on Monday night? Would you start Keenum or Bagent in week 4?

item.title: What’s next after Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson are placed on injured reserve?
item.description: This is fine. Who needs cornerbacks in the NFL?
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina Panthers have announced that Jaycee Horn (quadriceps) and Mike Jackson (groin) have been placed on injured reserve. That ends their season for at least the next four games, likely longer in at least Horn’s case. For those keeping track at home, Horn and Jackson formed one of the more formidable cornerback duos in the NFL and were the top two defensive backs on the Panthers team. Fifth year veteran Akayleb Evans, third year veteran Chau Smith-Wade, and rookie 4th round pick Will Lee III make up the entirety of the team’s current cornerback room.

Evans, Smith-Wade, and Lee have all flashed higher end talent in the past. Lee earned the starting nickel corner spot this offseason as a rookie and has had a number of near-highlight worthy plays paired with his fair share of rookie blunders. They all make for good depth at this point in their careers, but look for the Panthers to seek out veteran help in advance of this week’s Sunday Night Football match up against the Detroit Lions.

The veteran cornerback market is understandably thin at this point in the season. You have talented-but-injury-prone guys like Marshon Lattimore on the one hand, over-the-hill-journeymen like C.J. Goodwin (36) on the other, and guys with every other story in between. Dicaprio Bootle, who has not been on a 53-man roster since spending part of the 2024 season with the Los Angeles Chargers, may be the only veteran corner on the market currently with any direct experience with Ejiro Evero in Charlotte. Alph

Other free agent options include Bene Benwikere (35), (Eric Davis (58), Chris Gamble (43), Captain Munnerlyn (38, and still in Charlotte), Josh Norman (38), Melvin White (36). Second year corner and former undrafted free agent Corey Thornton is also currently on the team’s practice squad.

The long story short is that pickings are slim.

item.title: Early Week 4 NFL bets to make right now: 2 wagers that I like
item.description: Our NFL handicapper gives two Week 4 bets he likes at the moment.
item.content:encoded:
Heading into Week 4 of the NFL season, the biggest current storylines are the surprises in both some of the undefeated and winless teams.

There are five undefeated teams remaining: the Buffalo Bills, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs, Minnesota Vikings and … the Las Vegas Raiders. On the other end, the five teams without a win are the Miami Dolphins, Tennessee Titans, Tampa Bay Buccaneers … and the Houston Texans and Los Angeles Chargers.

For a fun exercise, I stacked together the closing lines of each moneyline and discovered the Raiders had a 7% chance of going 3-0, and the Chargers had a 2.8% chance of going 0-3.

Turning ahead to the Week 4 lines, there are two bets I think are worth betting immediately, and two more I am strongly considering betting.

Arizona Cardinals (-1.5, 44.5) at New York Giants

The Cardinals opened this week as 1.5-point underdogs and have been flipped to slight favorites. The early week market is backing the road Cardinals, and I very much agree.

New York's offense has completely stalled with Jameis Winston under center. Winston posted 111 passing yards on the road against the Rams, and then 118 yards at home versus the Tennessee Titans. The Giants rank 31st in passing yards per game now, and 28th in points per game. The inverse is a Cardinals offense that is much stronger than expectations and might still be a bit underrated in market. They average 33:14 time of possession (third in the NFL) and are converting 41% of their third downs.

Bet the Arizona Cardinals to beat the New York Giants at sportsbooks

The injury to star edge rusher Brian Burns is also a huge loss for the Giants, specific to this matchup. His presence would force Arizona to use tight end Trey McBride more in a blocking sense and not as an elite receiving threat as often. Jacoby Brissett will have clean pockets without as much pressure, and he thrives with time and makes few mistakes.

I model this game at Cardinals -1.4 prior to the injury adjustment to Burns. Let's move that out to -2, and then factor in the current pricing of the moneyline. While the spread is -1.5 (-105), the moneyline is only -112. Typically the gap between 1.5-point favorites and their respective moneylines should be 12 cents, and in this case its only 7 cents.

There is a discount here on the Cardinals ML, making this the best play on the Week 4 board.

Bet: Cardinals ML (-107)

Jacksonville Jaguars at Cincinnati Bengals (-2.5, 51.5)

The Jaguars are now 15-5 under head coach Liam Coen. I am comfortable saying Coen has entered the elite coaching tier. NFL fans spent years wondering if Trevor Lawrence was overrated or would ever reach his potential, but he has been playing just below an MVP level for more than an entire season now, and it seems switching from Urban Meyer and Doug Marrone to the innovative Coen was the trick.

Besides righting Lawrence, the Jaguars defense is supremely underrated. They have allowed a league-low 12 points per game (only three touchdowns in three games). They are also eighth in rushing yards allowed, seventh in sacks, third in takeaways and second in turnover differential. These are stats that are directly correlated to winning. I think the Jaguars have a coaching advantage, a defensive advantage and don't lag far behind in quarterback or skill position play, which the Bengals rely on as their strengths.

This line — currently at Jaguars +2.5 — feels like a floor price. I don't see a world where the Bengals hit the key number of -3, and the low vig on the Jaguars against the spread is worth taking on the chance this runs towards the Jaguars and closes around +1.5.

My numbers make this Jaguars +1.8, so a near vig free and expecting market support at +2.5 is enough room for me to play it. The correlated moneyline is around +117 with standard sportsbook hold, so I also like grabbing that at +120.

Bet: Jaguars +2.5 (-105) and ML +120

Rest of the games

The two bets I am strongly considering are the Indianapolis Colts and Green Bay Packers, both priced at -3.5. There is little urgency early in the week to bet a -3.5, as the chance it gets back to -3 would be far more crucial than playing a worse number at -4. The Colts have a clear coaching and run game advantage in an international road game against the Commanders, and the Packers have a rest and prep advantage going against an Tampa Bay's undrafted QB (Jalon Daniels) in his first start. The Packers are dealing with a bunch of injuries themselves, so the practice reports on Wednesday and Thursday will be critical in learning how to bet that game.

Check back later in the week for more additions to the Week 4 betting card.

item.title: Houston Texans NFL Power Rankings: Week 4
item.description: Where do the Texans fall after their loss to the Colts?
item.content:encoded:
The Houston Texans started this season with Super Bowl ambitions, and a large percentage of the NFL viewing public was behind them. Three weeks and three losses later, and this dream seems almost comical in hindsight. But, remarkably, the 12-5 squad from last year was in the same exact apocalyptic position at 0-3, and they went on the win nine straight! So, even though an 0-3 start is close to a death sentence, the Texans are technically not out of the race quite yet.

But, was does their 0-3 really say about this 2026 Texans team? How does it compare to last year’s squad?  Well, going back to my Week 4 Power Rankings of last year, I had a lot of similar things to say:

Punt after punt after punt (six in total for this game), hope deflated out of Texans fans like a balloon and was refilled by discontent and confusion. Why are so many receivers not getting open? Why is Stroud still getting pressured nearly every down? Why can’t the Texans get a rhythm going on offense? What in the WORLD are all these penalties about? – NFL Power Rankings Week 4 (2025)

Failing to get an offensive rhythm? Stroud getting pressured on every down? Sounds a lot like the complaints about Houston we’ve been hearing recently, but this doesn’t tell the whole story: In the first three games of the 2025 season, the Texans scored a total of just 38 points and failed to gain over 300 yards of offense in any of those contests. By contrast, the 2026 Texans have scored a total of 54 points in three games and have already broken the 300-yard mark twice so far. At first, this might yield some optimism on the Texans’ outlook for this season, but to still be 0-3 despite the modestly improved offense means the three losses may be more complicated, and not so easily repaired. The interior offensive line remains the primary culprit of Houston’s suffering, but the defense this season has not been quite as dominant as they were last year (at least so far), and combined with questionable time management by the coaching staff creates a recipe for a disastrous start to the season.

Houston fell out of most pundits’ top ten after their first loss, then they dropped into the middle of the standings after the second loss, and now following a third loss, the Texans may see their stock fall to its lowest point of the CJ Stroud/DeMeco Ryans era. This is going to be like ripping off a band-aid: here’s where the Houston Texans are ranked following their Week 3 loss to the Indianapolis Colts:

NFL.COM:

24. Houston Texans (0-3) 

The Texans have serious problems offensively that are painfully familiar. They can’t run the ball, lack difference-makers at receiver and still can’t consistently sustain drives. After a six-point output in the Week 2 loss to Cincinnati, the Texans were nearly as dreadful Sunday in Indianapolis, save for one urgent drive to briefly take a late lead. It’s unrealistic to expect the defense to carry Houston on a weekly basis, and until offensive coordinator Nick Caley finds some solutions, the Texans will remain mired in these struggles.

– Nick Shook

ESPN:

21. Houston Texans (0-3)

Week 3 result: Lost to the Colts 19-17
Week 3 ranking: 15

Fantasy surprise: RB David Montgomery

After scoring 28.9 fantasy points in Week 1, Montgomery has only 11.2 in the past two games combined. He averages 0.5 yards before contact — an abhorrent number for a rushing attack. Any hope for an improvement in Montgomery’s fantasy production starts with better play from the offensive line. That unit is a big reason the Texans are winless and averaging 11.5 points over the past two weeks.

– DJ Bien-Aime

SPORTS ILLUSTRATED:

16. Houston Texans (0–3) 

Last week’s ranking: No. 13
Last week’s result: lost to Colts, 19–17
This week: vs. Cowboys

When you get as involved in a team’s success as I did, the absolute breakdown of its most vulnerable unit—the one you believed would look brand new—feels especially difficult to stomach. But I would like to be a fly on the wall during the next phase of offensive meetings for the Houston Texans. Where is the machine coming unplugged?

– Conor Orr

BLEACHER REPORT:

27. Houston Texans (0-3)

Last Week: 16

Week 3 Result: Lost at Indianapolis 19-17

The good news is that the Texans are in familiar territory.

The bad news is that familiar territory is up a creek.

This marks the second straight season that the Texans have started 0-3. Last year, they rebounded to make the postseason and won a playoff game. The Texans also started 0-3 and made the playoffs in 2018.

But no team has made the playoffs after an 0-3 start in back-to-back seasons, and right now the Texans do not look the part of a contender—at all.

Houston’s offensive line play and rushing attack have been all but non-existent—against a Colts defense that entered Week 3 with the AFC’s worst defense, the Texans had 70 rushing yards and averaged less than 3.5 yards per carry. C.J. Stroud had his worst game of the season throwing the ball in Indianapolis.

Houston’s defense can’t do it all—and right now the offense isn’t doing much.

– Gary Davenport

CBS SPORTS:

27. Texans (0-3) (Last Week: 24)

At 0-3, their season is on the line against the Cowboys this week. The offense just isn’t good enough right now.

– Pete Prisco

USA TODAY:

25. Houston Texans (18): While he’s been hindered by key offensive absences, C.J. Stroud does not look like a quarterback deserving of a, say, $55 million-a-year contract.

– Nate Davis

YAHOO! SPORTS:

24. Houston Texans (0-3, LW: 19)

The Texans were 0-3 last season and went 12-5. So Houston can turn this around. But only six teams in NFL history, not counting the 1982 strike season, have made the playoffs after an 0-3 start, according to Josh Dubow of the Associated Press.

“0-3 is where we are right now,” Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans said, via Texans Wire. “The only way we can do anything about it is to go through it. We’re going through it right now, it’s adversity, it happens. For me, it starts with me. I have to do a better job of getting our guys ready to roll.”

The offense has been a problem. It has failed without Nico Collins, who has missed two games with a hamstring injury. Against a Colts defense that had allowed the most points and yards in the NFL through two weeks, the Texans had 93 yards through three quarters. And 68 of those yards, and seven of their eight first downs, came on one drive. Even with Collins out, it shouldn’t have been that hard to sustain drives. QB C.J. Stroud is looking for a contract extension, and the start to this season shouldn’t be providing the Texans any optimism that he’s worth the massive raise he’s seeking.

– Frank Schwab

THE ATHLETIC:

22. Houston Texans (0-3)

Last week: 17

Sunday: Lost to Colts 19-17

QB confidence: Falling, again

It’s been a roller-coaster ride for Houston fans and C.J. Stroud. In his first 23 games, Stroud was 15-8 with 26 touchdowns, five interceptions and a 101.7 passer rating. In the next 21 games, he was 9-12 with 11 touchdowns, nine interceptions and an 86.2 passer rating. Then another climb, seven straight wins that included nine touchdowns and four interceptions and a 91.5 passer rating. But now, Stroud has lost four straight games, and the Texans have started a second straight season 0-3.

Up next: vs. Cowboys, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET

– Chad Graff & Josh Kendall

PRO FOOTBALL TALK:

17. Texans (No. 10; 0-3): The offense needed to get a little bit better. Instead, the defense got more than a little bit worse.

– Mike Florio

Average Ranking: 22.56 (Last Week: 15.89)

If it makes you feel any better, Houston’s average rankings after last year’s 0-3 start was 20.78, and that clearly wasn’t indicative of how they finished the season. Last year, their swarming defense led that thrilling midseason resurgence, but what about this year? What could bring us optimism in these dark times of 2026?

Well, for me, I’m pining on the Texans steadily improving once again this year, which will be spurred this time by starters gradually returning from the injury report and new players improving as the season wears on. The return of WR Nico Collins and RG Ed Ingram should dramatically raise this offense’s ceiling and at least make CJ Stroud more productive. Another possible development of this season would be the improvement from rookie LG Keylan Rutledge and trade acquisition WR Kayshon Boutte, who hold within themselves the ability to transform this offense. If these four players can stay on the field and play complementary roles to each other, the Texans will start winning again.

What do you think, though? Will the Texans be able to actually right this ship in the 2026 season, or are they headed for troubled waters from which they will never return? What gives you optimism about this team, if any? Is a comeback like last year in the cards, or are they stuck in this rut until a serious change is made on the coaching staff, like offensive coordinator? Next week, the Texans will be hosting the Dallas Cowboys in a classic Texas battle, which could end up being Nick Caley’s last game if he fails to get the team over 20 points for the third time in a row. Could that be a blessing for this team, or a curse? Let us know your thoughts down in the comments below!

Go Texans!

The Daily Slop – 30 September 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders links

Articles

ESPN

Guard Sam Cosmi, safety Nick Cross out for London game vs. Colts

Guard Sam Cosmi and safety Nick Cross did not travel with the team to London on Tuesday night for their Week 4 game against the Colts.

Both were considered long shots to make the trip; each was hurt in Week 2 at Dallas. Cosmi suffered a concussion late in the 37-20 loss while Cross played despite an injury the team has described as “internal” but needed to have surgery after the game and stayed overnight at a hospital in Dallas.

With Cosmi once again sidelined, Nick Allegretti is expected to start at right guard with veteran Lucas Patrick at center. Patrick, signed after Week 1, left Sunday’s win with a boot on his left foot. He missed four snaps during the game because of an ankle injury.

A to Z Sports

Austin Ekeler returns and brings a lot to the table

Ekeler is known throughout the NFL as a strong leader in the locker room. He’s the type of player who contributes when he sees the field, regardless of snap count or role.

A depth move with stretch-run implications

This signing looks like a depth play on the surface, and it is one. But adding a player with Ekeler’s résumé and reputation carries weight beyond the stat sheet. Washington is building a backfield that can hold up over the course of a full season, and a veteran who understands his role and executes it well is exactly the kind of addition that pays off in December & January.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Riggo’s Rag

Charles Snowden signing could give Commanders timely help beyond the edge

Snowden has a lot of good football left at 28. He was an asset for the Las Vegas Raiders last season, recording three sacks, 28 tackles, two pass breakups, and an interception on 32 percent of the team’s defensive snaps.

Those are decent numbers, but an injury ended any hopes of the Virginia product making the Dallas Cowboys’ roster this summer.

Now, the Commanders are giving him a chance.

But there are concerns.

Snowden was suspended for the first three games of the 2026 campaign following a DUI. He is eligible to return this weekend, but that may be too soon for the Commanders. But if he fits in well over the coming days, the Silver Spring native might get elevated for Washington’s crunch divisional clash against the New York Giants in Week 5.

At 6-foot-6 and 250 pounds, Snowden has the size and length to make an impact. He sets a clean edge against the run and flashes explosiveness as a pass-rusher. But looking at the options available, the Commanders wouldn’t need him to be anything more than a complementary piece.

Odafe Oweh, K’Lavon Chaisson, and Dorance Armstrong Jr. lead the charge. Rookie fifth-rounder Joshua Josephs has also shown early promise, but the team may need him more at linebacker moving forward after Leo Chenal suffered a fractured neck that required season-ending surgery.

The Commanders aren’t losing much by finding out for sure what Snowden could offer.

And in all honesty, no team can ever have enough good players on the defensive front seven.

Last Man Standig

Sonny Styles has the green dot; should the Commanders take it back?

What’s the plan if Frankie Luvu returns?

I don’t mean whether Luvu returns to the starting lineup. That’s obvious — and quite good timing considering Washington’s linebacker depth has taken another hit with Leo Chenal’s neck injury. I’m talking about the green dot. Luvu handled those responsibilities in Week 1, and throughout the spring and summer. Styles took over the past two weeks after Luvu went down with a groin injury, while displaying the athletic gifts we saw at Ohio State and the NFL Scouting Combine.

To be clear, we’ve probably made too big a deal about the green dot at times. Having it means receiving the defensive call and communicating it to teammates. That’s important. It also frequently falls to a linebacker because of his position in the middle of the defense, not because the coaching staff has identified him as its resident Mensa member. But the circumstances make this particular decision interesting.

We now know Styles can handle it.

For more from Ben Standig, click here

Bullock’s Film Room (subscription)

Commanders Film Review: Sonny Styles vs Seahawks

[A]gainst the Seahawks, Chenal left the game with a devastating neck injury that requires surgery and will see him out for the rest of the season. With Luvu still out, Styles was partnered by second year linebacker Kain Medrano, who hadn’t played a snap on defense in his NFL career prior to this game.

Suddenly Styles was the experienced linebacker in the middle and fully responsible not just for relaying the plays from Daronte Jones, but making the adjustments at the line of scrimmage too. That’s a huge task to put on a rookie linebacker, especially considering the opposition. The Seahawks are the defending Super Bowl champions. Their offense is full of misdirection with multiple tight end sets, the ability to move star receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba all over the field, and a heavy dose of play-action passes and bootlegs.

It’s a lot to figure out mentally before the ball is even snapped, but despite all that, Styles put in his most impressive performance of the season so far. He was outstanding in coverage, intercepting a pass and breaking up another. He generated some effective pressure when blitzing and his run defense was solid too. So let’s break down his performance, starting with the highlights in coverage.

The Athletic (paywall)

Commanders first 3 games revealed what’s working, what still needs work

[P]er TruMedia, the Commanders have given up the third-fewest rushing yards per game (82.0). They also boast the lowest rate of first downs on opponent runs (15.6 percent), have the second-highest rate of opponent runs for zero or negative yards (28.1 percent) and are one of only five teams to not give up a rushing touchdown.

Eagles running back Saquon Barkley averaged 136.5 rushing yards and two rushing touchdowns in his four previous meetings with the Commanders (including the playoffs). But in the season opener, he totaled only 83 yards — 42 of which came on one run. He had four negative-yard rushes.

In Week 3, the Commanders gave up only 44 rushing yards to the Seahawks, only the second time since the start of the 2023 season that they allowed fewer than 50 in a game.

The biggest differences this season? The Commanders have given up only 2.9 yards per run on first and second downs, compared to 4.9 and 4.8 yards in 2025 and ‘24, respectively. They’ve also gotten to opposing rushers quickly, hitting them at or behind the line of scrimmage on 56.3 percent of their runs to yield only 0.61 yards before contact per rush.

Lucas Patrick at center

The 10-year veteran signed with the Commanders on Sept. 16 and was thrust into the starting lineup 11 days later as Mariota’s center.

Guard Sam Cosmi was out with a concussion, so instead of turning to rookie Matt Gulbin or elevating Julian Good-Jones from the practice squad, the Commanders put Patrick at center and shifted Nick Allegretti to right guard.

Patrick fought through an ankle injury to play 65 of the team’s 69 offensive snaps, and allowed two pressures and zero sacks.

Sports Illustrated

With Leo Chenal out for the season, Jonathan Taylor presents the next challenge in London

Rookie Sonny Styles played in all 67 defensive snaps last week, while Kain Medrano played 44 of 67 defense snaps after Chenal’s injury. The team may have to lean heavily on the two again if Luvu can’t play Sunday.

Washington faces an opponent Sunday who has had a lot of success on the ground so far, with the Colts averaging 103.3 yards a game and Jonathan Taylor rushing for 258 yards and four rushing touchdowns on 66 carries through three games. That total includes 98 yards against Baltimore and 92 yards and two touchdowns against Kansas City. Taylor also has nine receptions for 67 yards, bringing his total yards from scrimmage to 325.

While the passing defense has been a problem that opposing offenses have teed off on because of obvious communication issues, that shouldn’t take away from the success they found facing the rush. It’s also only been three games. Sunday will present the defense with another challenge: stopping Jonathan Taylor without one of the players specifically brought in to help establish it.

The pass rush, led by edge defenders Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Kayvon Thibodeaux, and supplemented by athletic inside linebackers as well as defensive backs capable of blitzing, was supposed to be the strength of the Giants’ defense. After Case Keenum’s stunning performance, Bears have QB dilemma: Who should start?

Keenum is still the team’s No. 3 quarterback. And with Tyson Bagent clearing concussion protocol over the weekend, the door remains open for him to get his first start since 2023 as Caleb Williams continues rehabilitating from his hamstring strain.

Yet is it really practical for coach Ben Johnson to turn so quickly to Bagent after Keenum’s performance Monday in such a convincing win — 247 passing yards, two touchdown passes, plus a TD run with no sacks and no turnovers? Johnson wouldn’t offer comment Tuesday during his interview on ESPN Radio 1000 other than that they will see how things play out.

That’s the riddle being solved at Halas Hall this week and a brain teaser we’re trying to sound out.

When better players and better options are available, you take that route. But Monday night felt like something more than just a relief-filled home win in Williams’ absence. Keenum brought purpose to the huddle and magic to the air, operating the offense at a high level, getting the ball where it needed to go and managing the game with poise.

Conventional wisdom would be to stick with the guy who excelled in primetime against Vic Fangio’s defense. Or is conventional wisdom that Bagent is ahead of Keenum on the depth chart and he should start with a full week of practice? One thing Johnson is emphatic about, though, is that every week is a new week. Just because Keenum lit the Eagles up doesn’t mean he’ll do the same to the Jets, especially on short rest.

We should step back for a moment — considering the history of bad Bears quarterbacks, what an incredible problem to have. The Bears finally have “the guy” in Williams. He gets hurt. His backup gets concussed, and the No. 3 has one of the greatest fill-in performances in team history. And now the city will debate which backup should start while feeling good about both.

How NFL players cope with CTE risks, fears and internal debates

ESPN asked more than 30 active and retired players how the increased attention on brain trauma has affected their lives and career decisions. All were aware of CTE to at least a small degree, an advantage that thousands of their predecessors did not have. Some acknowledged CTE has become a topic of dark humor, including Pittsburgh Steelers safety DeShon Elliott: “Sometimes you might draw a blank and forget something from last week and you go, ‘Oh my god, it’s that CTE.'”

[S]ome players follow what they consider best practices to minimize their chances of getting CTE. NFL rules changes and attempts to improve equipment — such as Guardian Caps — instill confidence in some players. Others consider brain health out of their hands and ultimately an acceptable tradeoff for the benefits of an NFL career.

“I think [for] any football player, that crosses your mind,” said 26-year-old Arizona Cardinals receiver Michael Wilson, who’s in his fourth season. “But also, that is so far down the line and … the legacy, the financial gain that you can carve out for yourself to me outweighs the risk of CTE, especially as a wideout.

“How cool would it be to leave a legacy that generations of my family, the Wilson legacy will talk about? And if CTE is a consequence of that, then so be it. But I also could sleep good at night knowing that I was the one person in the Wilson family that ended up changing our financial, socioeconomic class, like you can point it back to me and say, ‘Michael’s the one that did it.’ So for my kids’ kids’ kids’ kids, they can always look at me and if CTE is a consequence of that, then I’m willing to bet on myself that hopefully I won’t get it, but if I do, then I made a decision and I chose that.”

Weeks after the interview, Wilson signed a three-year, $75 million extension.

item.title: 49ers in review: The offense is off to a historic start
item.description: And we all know why the 49ers are off to this historic start
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers moved to 3-0 on the season and 2-0 in the NFC West with a 36-30 win over the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. 

At one point, it seemed the 49ers would run away with the game but instead played with their food a little bit, allowing the Cardinals to sneak back into the game late. San Francisco were able to stave off Arizona, securing a needed victory before the schedule gets tough with the Broncos and Seahawks on the horizon. 

But before we look too far ahead, let’s take one last look at Week 3 and review what we can learn going into Week 4 and beyond:

Brock Purdy is the league MVP… through 3 games

You can tell that Purdy is feeling himself when he’s trying a jump pass along the sideline. That was simply a heat check for the quarterback. But 49ers fans can also see that Purdy is playing out of his mind.

With his four-touchdown performance in Week 3 against Arizona, Purdy closed one of the best three-game stretches. Sunday marked the third time in Purdy’s career where he’s gone a stretch of three games with nine or more passing touchdowns and one or fewer interceptions:

  • Weeks 13-15, 2023: 10 touchdowns, 1 interception
  • Weeks 13-16, 2025: 9 touchdowns, 1 interception
  • Weeks 1-3, 2026: 9 touchdowns, 1 interception

But what makes this stretch so impressive is how he’s doing it with such a hampered receiver room. After Mike Evans went out with an injury in the second quarter, Purdy was without his top four receivers (Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, Ricky Pearsall, and Demarcus Robinson) and didn’t target Deebo Samuel once. Despite it all, Purdy completed 8-of-12 passes for 127 yards and a pair of touchdowns.

It helps that George Kittle exists, but Purdy was moving downfield with Jordan Watkins, who was banished to the shadow realm just a week ago. 

Maybe it’s just a hot three games, and he settles a bit, but maybe this is who Brock Purdy is now. And if that’s the case, his MVP case will only get stronger as the season goes on. 

And the 49ers offense is having a historically good start because of Purdy

Purdy’s hot start has worked wonders for the 49ers offense. They’ve not only produced the most points scored through three games under Kyle Shanahan, but with their 36 points on Sunday, the 49ers are up to 98 points this season, one of the hottest starts in franchise history:

  1. 1949 – 115 points
  2. 1998 – 112 points
  3. 1948 – 112 points
  4. 1983 – 107 points
  5. 1965 – 103 points
  6. 2026 – 98 points

Maybe something to note: the 49ers have never won a Super Bowl in a season where they scored more than 100 points in its first three games. San Francisco has, however, won two Super Bowls (1984 and 1994) when scoring between 95-99 points in the first three games, so Shanahan might have found the sweet spot.

But, look at some of the quarterbacks who led the offenses above: John Brodie in 1965, Joe Montana in 1983, and Steve Young in 1998. Some of the greatest in 49ers history. And now it’s Purdy who has led the 2026 offense to a historic start.

Out of curiosity, I looked at how this start compares to when Shanahan led the Atlanta Falcons to a franchise-high 540 points in 2016 with an offense that featured the league MVP Matt Ryan, Julio Jones, and Devonta Freeman. That Falcons team scored 104 points through its first three games of that season. This 49ers team is just one touchdown behind that pace. 

This isn’t to say the 49ers are going to score 534 points through 17 games (the franchise record is 505 points, though), but just to put into context just how good of a start the San Francisco offense is. Is it sustainable? We’ll find out. But these three games are all we have to go off of, and so far, so good. 

Oh, and don’t forget the offensive line

Purdy and the offense’s success can be tracked back to the most scrutinized position group entering the regular season: the offensive line. That success continued against the Cardinals on Sunday. 

I mean, where do you want to start? The fact that the 49ers are the only team to not allow a sack yet this season or the 49ers have only had four plays from scrimmage that resulted in negative yards (non-kneels)? Both of those can be traced back to the front five.

Purdy has only been pressured on a quarter of his 90 dropbacks this season. When he is pressured, he’s only completed 43 percent of his passes, but he’s yet to make a mistake. But on the 75 percent of the dropbacks he’s been kept clean, Purdy has been nearly flawless, throwing all nine of his touchdowns with a passer rating of 142.8. 

It can only help the confidence that Purdy has been exuding, knowing that three-fourths of the time, he’s going to have time to find the open receiver he has seemingly on every play.

But the offensive line is getting it done in the run game as well. The only four negative plays the 49ers offensive line has allowed this season are:

  • a Christian McCaffrey run for a loss of three on Sunday
  • a Kaelon Black run for a loss of two on Sunday
  • a McCaffrey reception for a loss of one in Week 1
  • a Black run for a loss of one in Week 2

The offensive line has been as good as anybody could have asked through three weeks. It makes sense that the 49ers have scored on nearly 60 percent of their offensive drives this season, because the offensive line keeps the offense moving forward. 

Pass rushers needed

Yes, Nick Bosa and Mykel Williams should be back within the next few weeks. Sure, the Matt Judon addition helps. But the 49ers are going to need more than that. Much, much more than that.

For the 49ers fans here that pay attention to the San Francisco Giants, the 49ers pass rush reminds me of the 2026 Giants bullpen. Everybody knew the Giants bullpen needed help entering the season, but Buster Posey and the Giants front office didn’t do anything to address the need, and unsurprisingly, the Giants bullpen was bad.

The same could be said for the 49ers pass rush. After a 20-sack season in 2025, all the 49ers did in the offseason was draft Romello Height and wait for Bosa to get healthy, and that was enough on the edges, banking on Bosa staying healthy.

Sunday against Arizona, the Bosa-less pass rush pressured Jacoby Brissett 14 times on 54 dropbacks, sacking him twice. Even with Bosa, the 49ers pass rush wasn’t showing much, recording zero sacks in Week 1, and while the 49ers sacked Malik Willis four times in Week 2, two of those sacks were Willis running himself out of bounds behind the line of scrimmage.

The talent gap needs to be significantly closer between Bosa and whoever you would have as the 49ers’ second pass rusher. Judon closes that gap a little bit, but Judon didn’t have a sack in 368 snaps for the Dolphins and Bills last season and hasn’t recorded a sack since Week 17 of the 2024 season. 

Maybe there’s a pass rusher out there, and let’s just choose a name at random here; let’s say the Chase Young skill range would help close that gap. John Lynch and company have until Tuesday, November 10, at 1 p.m. to find help on the edges.

item.title: Wink Martindale offers to help "outclassed" Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker
item.description: Coaching inexperience is holding the Cowboys back.
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys' failure to beat the Ravens in Rio came from all three phases of the team. The offense failed to turn first and goal from the two with 20 seconds left into a game-winning touchdown, the special teams served up favorable field position on the kickoff after the game-tying field goal, and the defense allowed the Ravens to gain enough yards to set up the game-winning field goal.

The ultimate blame resides with coach Brian Schottenheimer, who shouldn't be learning the job of being an effective head coach while on the job.

Still, the defense continues to be a problem. Long-time NFL and college defensive coach Wink Martindale spoke bluntly about the situation during his latest appearance on Talkin' Ball with Pat Leonard.

"I don't want to be an asshole but he’s being outclassed right now," Martindale said regarding Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker. "So Jerry [Jones] can call me and I'll go help him. But, you know, I'm talking about helping the coordinator."

Matching a head coach who is learning the job on the fly with a defensive coordinator who is learning the job on the fly isn't ideal. It would have been useful for Schottenheimer, who has no former NFL head coaches on his staff, to have access to a key lieutenant who has done the job of head coach before — and whose experiences can help Schottenheimer realize the right answers to the test before he turns the paperwork in.

That's really the problem with the Cowboys. They lack the ability to prepare for the unique situations that experienced coaches know how to address. It played out on Sunday, giving the Cowboys a loss that could echo into January

And that could be the difference between making it to the playoffs or going home after Week 18, for the third straight season.

item.title: Andrew Luck still has no regrets about early NFL retirement: 'I’m right where I’m supposed to be'
item.description: Andrew Luck's retirement in 2019 remains a fascinating topic for football fans.
item.content:encoded:
Andrew Luck has always seemed more content about his early NFL retirement than the rest of us.

It seems like Luck retired just a bit ago, but it has been a while. More time has passed since Luck’s retirement in 2019 (2,594 days) than the length of his NFL career (2,540 days from his debut to retirement). And yet, Luck still remains a curious figure because of the abruptness and surprise of his retirement, which he said was due to an unrelenting cycle of injuries and rehab. He’s just 37 years old. Kirk Cousins, who has helped the Las Vegas Raiders to a 3-0 start and was in the 2012 NFL Draft like Luck, is 38.

For a few years after the retirement it was a pastime of fans to project a Luck comeback every time a quarterback got hurt, but that comeback never happened. Luck is happy with his job as the general manager of Stanford’s football program. And he said this week he has no regrets.

“Nope,” Luck said during an interview with Yahoo Sports Daily. “Not to say it wasn’t a hard [decision], it was the hardest decision of my life probably up until that point, and maybe since as well, but no. It was exactly what needed to happen for me. Again, not an easy one, but the right one.”

Had Luck never retired, he could still be playing and presumably doing so at a high level. Matthew Stafford, who won his first MVP last season, is a year older than Luck. But Luck will let everyone else worry about what might have happened, because he doesn’t do so himself.

Andrew Luck watched Philip Rivers from afar

Plenty of quarterbacks get the itch to return. Philip Rivers was coaching high school football when he came out of retirement to play for the Indianapolis Colts late last season. Drew Brees said he thought about coming out of retirement for the Denver Broncos when they lost Bo Nix to injury before the AFC championship game last season, and texted Denver assistants Pete Carmichael and Joe Lombardi, his offensive coordinator and quarterback coach when he was with the Saints.

Rivers is seven years older than Luck, and didn’t have the history with the Colts that Luck did. But Luck says the Colts didn’t call him asking about a return.

“I have an amazing relationship with Chris Ballard, the GM of the Colts, amazing,” Luck told Yahoo Sports Daily. “I consider him a mentor of mine, we have been through some ‘ish’ together and come out the other side and have a stronger relationship, so no. We are on the same page there.”

Luck was interested in watching though. He said he was at a 49ers game with recently hired Stanford head coach Tavita Pritchard during Rivers’ first game back since 2020, and was watching the Colts play the Seahawks on his iPhone.

“Like 99.9% of America, I was fascinated by Philip coming back and playing, and playing at a high level, and doing it as a grandfather,” Luck said.

He just didn’t have the desire to do it himself.

Luck has ‘no regrets’

If Luck had continued to play, and was paid at or near the top of the quarterback pay scale every season since his retirement, he would have made more than $400 million more in career earnings from the NFL and counting.

Most people couldn’t fathom stepping away from the fame and fortune of being an NFL quarterback just before you turn 30 years old, with perhaps a decade left to play. Then there’s Luck, who reacted to a question about stepping away from the NFL by saying he was “stoked” about an espresso he just had.

“No regrets, and not to say I did things perfectly by any stretch of the imagination,” Luck told Yahoo Sports Daily. “I learned a bunch from both the successful moments and the low moments of playing as a professional quarterback and for the Colts. But I think, life keeps moving forward. Thankful for the opportunites I had and I also feel full of purpose and passion as the general manager of Stanford football. I love this school, I love this program, there’s a real mission we’re on. I love working with these young men. I love our coaching staff.

“I’m right where I’m supposed to be. I have an amazing wife and two amazing daughters. Life keeps throwing wonderful pleasant gifts along the way.”

After some years completely out of the spotlight, Luck came back to football with Stanford. He said he still believes in the character development that comes along with the sport. But he understands the darker side of football. When Joe Burrow wondered aloud last season, after multiple injuries, why he’d keep playing football if it wasn’t fun anymore, everyone made the comparison to Luck stepping away right in his prime. Luck knows the toll the game can take.

“I think the majority of professional athletes go through questions like this at various points in their career,” Luck said, when asked about Burrow. “That’s part of being a professional athlete. Especially in a trying, violent — football is not a contact sport, it’s a collision sport, and it can be trying.”

And Luck had enough of that life as a player. He hasn’t looked back.

item.title: Scouting New York Jets offensive lineman Jordan Meredith
item.description: Taking a look at the Jets’ recently acquired interior offensive lineman
item.content:encoded:
The Jets recently acquired former Raiders offensive lineman Jordan Meredith via trade. Today, we break Meredith down in detail.

The 28-year old Meredith is listed at 6’2” and 300 pounds and was undrafted out of Western Kentucky in 2021. He has started 20 games in his NFL career, all of them with the Las Vegas Raiders. He played on special teams with the Jets in the first two games of this season, but saw extensive action on offense in the fourth quarter of the Lions game due to an injury.

Background

Meredith was a two-star high school recruit, who headed to Western Kentucky in 2016 and redshirted his first season before serving as a backup in 2017. From 2018 through 2020, he started all 37 games earning an all-Conference USA honorable mention in 2019 and second-team recognition in 2020.

His NFL career began as an undrafted free agent with the Rams, for whom he did not make the roster or practice squad in 2021.

Meredith spent most of the 2022 season on the Raiders’ practice squad, although he was also briefly on the Browns’ practice squad as well. He ended up making his NFL debut with Las Vegas, albeit only seeing action on special teams.

Over the past three seasons, his role increased. He played in every game and made his first NFL start in 2023, then began the season as a reserve but ultimately started eight games in 2024. At the start of the 2025 season, he was named as the starting center and he started the first nine games there before moving back to guard for two games and then landing on injured reserve.

The Jets acquired Meredith at the end of preseason, in exchange for a future year pick swap.

Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Meredith brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study.

Measurables/Athleticism

Meredith lacks ideal size and has poor length, which is perhaps why the Raiders were keen to try him at the center position, even moving their previous starting center out to guard to accommodate this.

His workout numbers were really good, with a 5.11 in the 40-yard dash, 25 bench press reps and good agility and explosiveness numbers.

Usage

In college, Meredith only played right guard other than one snap which saw him listed at left tackle. At the NFL level he had some preseason experience at center before the Raiders moved him permanently ahead of the 2025 season. He has otherwise seen plenty of action at both guard spots, and indeed moved back to guard for a couple of games in 2025 before landing on injured reserve.

Pass Blocking

Meredith’s individual pass protection numbers have been solid throughout most of his college and pro careers. He has a low pressure rate and doesn’t give up many sacks.

In 2018 and 2020, he only gave up one sack. However, 2019 may have been his best season for pass protection even though he alllowed three sacks. He only gave up four other pressures all year and his pass protection grade according to Pro Football Focus led the nation.

His numbers were solid with the Raiders too, as he only gave up two sacks in his first 18 starts. He did give up three sacks in his final two starts of last season, but that was right before he went on injured reserve, so he may have been limited at the time. Also, those were the two games after he moved from center back to guard, which may have been a factor. The Raiders gave up 10 sacks in one of those games, as the Browns created constant pressure with stunts.

Meredith has good feet and is capable of mirroring to stay in front of his man and a good sense of how to direct his man to prevent leverage advantages.

He can anchor against a bull rush but if he loses leverage, he may lack the physical tools to recover.

Run Blocking

Meredith doesn’t necessarily bring power and drive as a run blocker, but he’s athletic enough to make blocks on the move and is good at finding a target in space and angling his man off.

In addition, he is also a good pulling option with the athleticism to make reach blocks on the move.

As noted, he’s not consistently powerful at the point of attack. However, he does work well on combo blocks.

Short Yardage

The Raiders’ record at the goal line with Meredith at center was not good last year. In fact, they only had three rushing touchdowns of less than 50 yards all season, from three, three and four yards. However, he did a decent job on this play.

They fared slightly better in that category in 2024 when he was at guard, rushing for three one-yard touchdowns, including a quarterback sneak, in his eight starts.

Screen Blocking

Meredith clearly has the athleticism to get out in front of a screen pass and has impressed with his ability to block in space.

Footwork/Technique

Meredith moves his feet well to stay in front of rushers and has a decent punch and anchor, although he perhaps over-compensates for his lack of size by over-extending himself at times in the drive phase.

His arms were measured at just 31 inches which would be in the bottom 10 for offensive line scouting combine measurements over the past 27 years. This doesn’t tend to affect him once he’s locked onto a block because can extend his arms and lock his elbows to keep his man at bay. He also resets his hands constantly in pass protection. However, he can be slow to get those hands up at times.

This also affected him when he was at the center position, because by the time he had snapped the ball and got his hands up, his man was often too quick for him.

Penalties

Meredith showed a good improvement in terms of his on-field discipline during his college career, reducing his offensive penalty count from eight, to six and then four over the course of his three years as a starter.

Penalties haven’t been a major issue during his NFL career either, as he has only been called for seven. Only one of these was a holding call and none were personal fouls.

Special Teams

Meredith’s only special teams role at the NFL level has been as a blocker on the placekicking unit. This was also the case in college, apart from four plays where he was on the punt protection unit.

He had one special teams penalty in college.

Instincts/Intelligence

Meredith has displayed versatility at the NFL level and is considered to have good awareness and football IQ. He is also regarded as a good communicator.

However, at times last year, the Raiders line was in chaos, as they really struggled to pick up stunts. Prior to that, Meredith had shown that he can pick up a basic stunt effectively while at the guard position, so he may not have been the main culprit in that.

Meredith is definitely not immune to mental errors, though. On this short yardage play, he clearly expected everyone else to downblock and the nose tackle was able to capitalize on him moving out of the way.

He has had three pre-snap penalties at the NFL level, all of them on false starts. He was also called three times for being an illegal man downfield on a pass.

Attitude

Meredith apparently has some nastiness to his game and a killer instinct in terms of his finishing and aggressiveness.

By moving around so much, he has displayed adaptability and a team-first attitude, and his resilience to establish himself with the Raiders having been released five times at the NFL level has been impressive.

Injuries

Meredith has had some ankle issues during his career, which led to him being placed on injured reserve last season. He had also been limited by an ankle issue during the 2024 season at times.

Scheme Fit

The Jets have clearly brought Meredith in to be their fourth interior lineman as it seems likely he would be the first man off the bench at all three interior positions. The team’s unofficial website lists him as the number two at all three spots.

Ultimately, though, all three current starters can play center, so Meredith won’t necessarily have to move there if someone does get hurt.

He has been a teammate of current Jets players Geno Smith, Dylan Parham and Tyler Johnson while he with the Raiders. He was also a teammate of Troy Reeder when he was with the Rams.

Conclusions

Meredith’s fate with the Raiders was probably sealed once they brought in Tyler Linderbaum, but the Jets will hope he gives them a viable backup option. He even accepted a paycut following the trade.

In 2024, it looked like Meredith was establishing himself as one of the Raiders’ young building blocks. Based on Pro Football Focus grades, he was a top-10 guard in the NFL that season.

The move to center didn’t go too well, but the Raiders’ offensive line as a whole was a mess last season so it’s difficult to say whether he is incapable of playing well at that position, or just had a difficult time as the anchor of poorly performing unit.

As was the case with Parham, the Jets will be hoping that Meredith is a better player than he showed in 2025 and, if that’s the case, he gives them a solid reserve option for the rest of this season and the fact he has familiarity with Smith and Parham is probably a bonus, even though they were collectively involved in the Raiders’ struggles last season.

Meredith may be about to get an extended look in place of Parham, as we await news on the severity of the injury he suffered in Sunday’s game.

item.title: Seahawks Week 4 power rankings: A fall from the top after surprise loss to Commanders
item.description: The Seahawks are no longer the national media darlings of the NFC West.
item.content:encoded:
Entering Week 3, the Seattle Seahawks were widely considered the best team in the NFL. However, when you are on top of the mountain, there is only one way to go; down. After losing to the Washington Commanders last week, the Seahawks will very likely slip down the national media power rankings this week. However, how far will they slip? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (B/R), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle.

Both NFL.com and B/R have dropped the Seahawks down to 4th. In their ranking, NFL.com noted that Seattle’s turnovers (two from Sam Darnold, and one from Jadarian Price) were the big differences against the Commanders. An interesting thing to note as well is that NFL.com ranks the San Francisco 49ers as the new number one team in the NFL. BR meanwhile brought up the Seahawks inability to run the ball effectively in Washington. Seattle ran for less than 50 yards and only 2.4 yards per carry in last week’s loss.

ESPN was the only national media site last week to not rank the Seahawks first in the NFL. However, this week ESPN did not penalize the team too much, only dropping Seattle from 2nd to 4th. In their ranking, ESPN also discussed Price’s underwhelming start. Price ranks 47th in the NFL in fantasy points among running backs – although some of that can also be credited to Seattle deploying a timeshare in the backfield. Regardless, Price’s fumbling issues will likely not help with the timeshare problem. 

CBS dropped the Seahawks four spots, from first to fifth in the NFL. CBS noted that despite the interceptions from Darnold, he still “did some good things in his return” and that the Seahawks will be back after this surprising loss. CBS did not issue the biggest drop in power rankings. That honor belongs to PFT, who dropped the Seahawks from first all the way to sixth best in the league. PFT did not offer much analysis in their ranking other than “we’ll find out soon whether the loss at Washington was an aberration or a harbinger.” 

Overall, as can be expected after an upset loss to a team with a backup quarterback, the Seahawks dropped in the national media power rankings. Entering week three, the average power ranking between the five polled sites was 1.2. Entering week four, that average has dropped to 4.6. 

Despite the loss, the league is still high on the Seahawks. A loss this season was inevitable. Perhaps it is better to get it out of the way early against a non-NFC West team. The Seahawks next test will be in week four against the desperate Los Angeles Chargers. Let’s see if Seattle can get back on track, or if this time next week we are discussing why the team is slipping down the power rankings once again.

item.title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers trying to dig out of a hole
item.description: The Packers have given themselves a lot to fix.
item.content:encoded:
You’ve got no shortage of bad things to choose from during the early days of the season, but one of the worst things about the Packers stumbling out of the gate is that everyone else in the NFC North has as well.

The Vikings lost their starting quarterback early in Week 1, but the Packers couldn’t take advantage — as we well know. They let the Vikings survive, and now they’re 3-0.

The Bears, meanwhile, lost their own quarterback a week later, dropping a game to the Vikings as a result. They managed to keep things afloat the following week, but they remain vulnerable.

The Lions, for their part, have staggered to a 1-2 start, the same as the Packers.

All of this, of course, was avoidable. The Packers went into the season with a patchwork offensive line — and we’re being offensive to patchwork quilters with that description. They have more self respect than the Packers showed trotting out that bunch. But that’s beside the point. It didn’t have to be this way. They’re taking steps now to fix it, but there was no need to wait. 

Kevin Zeitler was sitting at home for all of training camp, as was Mekhi Becton. Laken Tomlinson’s been chilling on the Cowboys’ practice squad, too. Sure, there have been some unexpected bumps in the road — nobody planned for Aaron Banks to battle an injury for weeks and weeks and weeks, and nobody expected Zach Bako-Bewele’s knee to implode — but there was plenty of opportunity to mitigate those possibilities before things turned into a disaster. 

Now the Packers have dug themselves a hole. They’re trying to dig out, but it’s better to not put yourself in a hole to begin with.

item.title: Billy Edwards Jr. will make or break UNC’s chances against Notre Dame
item.description: After a subpar performance against Clemson, Bill Belichick needs his starting QB to step up against the Irish.
item.content:encoded:
Heading into Week 5’s matchup against the #3-ranked Notre Dame Fighting Irish, there is one player who Coaches Belichick and Petrino need to call upon to be better and step up as the team’s leader and X-factor.

It’s not an overly complex observation.

Quarterback Billy Edwards Jr. has to be better if North Carolina is to stand a chance.

Edwards in Weeks 1 and 2

In the first two games of the 2026 season, Billy Edwards was good and at times almost great. His reputation coming into the season was that of an experienced quarterback who doesn’t blow you away with his athleticism, but can stand in the pocket, make good decisions, and lead an offense down the field. He generally avoids turnovers and the kind of mistakes that can flip a game on its head, but he’s also unlikely to blow the top off the stadium.

He’s a lot less Michael Vick and a lot more Joe Flacco.

And through the first two games of the season, he looked the part. Against TCU in Ireland, he only posted a 57.1% completion rate, but he avoided any crucial turnovers that could have altered the 15-10 final score in TCU’s favor.

Against ETSU, he comfortably completed 15/20 passes for 244 yards and 2 TDs and led a balanced attack up and down Chris Smith Field that allowed his running backs to feast for 161 rushing yards and 3 TDs.

After the first two games, it was apparent the 2026 version of Billy Edwards was still not flashy. Those behind him on the depth chart likely possess greater talent and higher upside. But he is a quarterback you can trust to win ballgames the boring way.

Traveling Down to Clemson

The road trip down to Clemson, South Carolina, brought new challenges for Edwards.

The game started off well enough. Touchdown drive followed by touchdown drive followed by back-to-back field goal attempts. With 8:36 left in the 2nd quarter, Edwards had the Tar Heel offense up 17-3, the Clemson fans were booing their own team, and Edwards looked comfortable navigating whatever packages Clemson’s defense threw at him.

And then, it all just flipped.

  • 3-and-out to end the 2nd quarter.
  • 3-and-out to start the 3rd quarter
  • Fumble by the running back on the first play from scrimmage
  • 6 plays, 22 yards gained, Punt
  • 3-and-out
  • 12 plays, 60 yards gained, Field Goal
  • Turnover on downs
  • Interception

In the first half, Edwards completed 7/15 passing for 83 yards and 1 TD (5.5 yards/attempt). In the second half, Edwards completed 6/15 passes for 52 yards and 0 TDs (3.5 yards/attempt). The drop-off in yards per attempt is noticeable, but does not explain the difference in outcome on its own.

The rushing game was comparable in both halves: 19 attempts for 112 yards (5.9 yards/carry) in the first half and 20 attempts for 102 yards (5.1 yards/carry) in the second half. North Carolina didn’t move away from the run game, and the run game didn’t stop being effective.

So what changed?

The boring, not-so-flashy quarterback helming the offense stopped converting on third down.

In both halves, North Carolina attempted 7 third-down conversions. In the first half, the offense converted 4 of 7. In the second half, they only converted one third down, which did not come until the final drive of the game.

First half third downs: 4 of 7, 57%

UNC converted:

  • 3rd-and-6: Edwards to Shipp, 23 yards
  • 3rd-and-2: Demon June, 4-yard run
  • 3rd-and-6: Edwards to Hall, 15-yard TD
  • 3rd-and-6: Edwards scramble/run, 17 yards

Three of those four conversions came on drives that produced points.

Second-half third downs: 1 of 7, 14%

UNC failed on:

  • 3rd-and-4: incomplete
  • 3rd-and-9: incomplete
  • 3rd-and-5: sack
  • 3rd-and-8: 7-yard completion, one yard short
  • 3rd-and-4: zero-yard June run
  • 3rd-and-2: one-yard Hall run

Sprinkle in no passing plays of 15+ yards in the second half (three 15+ yard passing plays in the first half), and you end up with an offense that can’t stay on the field.

Edwards did not turn the ball over until the final drive. But he could not find ways to move the chains or create big plays in the second half.

Turning Towards Notre Dame

So why is Billy Edwards the X-Factor against Notre Dame?

Because he was the single point of failure against Clemson.

The running game remained strong in both halves. The defense softened in the second half, but not excessively. It was Edwards’ inability to create and sustain momentum that doomed the Tar Heels.

Edwards needs to not panic against Notre Dame and be the boring quarterback. He needs to protect the football and avoid turnovers against a defense that will be tougher and meaner than anything he’s faced this season.

But he also needs to be a downfield threat. He needs to convert on third down. He needs to find ways to keep his offense on the field.

If he can do that, the Notre Dame game could look a lot more like the first half of the Clemson game.

Touchdown.

Touchdown.

Field Goal Attempt.

Field Goal Attempt.

17-3 Tar Heels with 8:36 left in the half.
