item.title: Fantasy Football: Why has this season been so unpredictable (Kalif Raymond?!) — let's investigate
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen shares some data-driven observations of the NFL season thus far.
item.content:encoded:
Comparing the NFL season to a roller coaster is a cliché for a reason. There are peaks and valleys. The twists and turns you "know" are coming can still catch you by surprise. And then it's all over before you fully take in what happened.

Shoot, that describes just Sunday's action, let alone a full season.

But as fantasy football managers, we don't get to just enjoy the ride. We have to figure out where the track is going. Data or film can make us think we're heading one way. And then an errant throw, missed block or dropped pass can change everything. On a larger scale, poor in-game decisions or an ill-timed penalty can be the difference between a winning record and a losing one.

This coaster is already on the move, and I'd be lying if I said I knew where it was going. But, through a few teams and some player arcs, let's sift through what we've seen and get an idea of what to expect in the short term.

Win-loss records are only part of the story

Last season was an extreme case, but it's not uncommon for playoff teams to have slow starts. Half of the divisional-round participants in 2025 were 1-2 or worse (Houston had three losses!). So, as Sunday night highlighted, position in the standings at this point isn't always the best barometer of future talent.

Take the Rams, for instance.

Matthew Stafford responds RIGHT BACK to give the Rams the lead 🤯

L.A. and Denver are going back and forth in the 4th 💥

(via @NFL)

pic.twitter.com/he9ljc1qye

— Yahoo Sports (@YahooSports) September 28, 2026

We've now seen three versions of the Rams offense. Tired in Australia, facing off against Jameis Winston and in a back-and-forth matchup with Denver. Each has its own microcosm of nuance, but the constant on offense is Matthew Stafford. And the Broncos highlighted a weakness in his game.

  • Week 1 (when under pressure): 20.0% (Completion Rate), 12.2 (aDOT), 3.22 (Average Time to Throw)

  • Week 2: 50.0%, 8.8, 2.64

  • Week 3: 39.1%, 11.3, 2.95

Nobody's immune to getting rattled in the pocket. But Stafford sitting behind Cam Ward, C.J. Stroud and Malik Willis in EPA per dropback when under duress seems problematic. That's where the loss of Terrance Ferguson (for at least Week 4) becomes an issue. Half of Stafford's attempts when the Giants got through the line went to the second-year TE at shallower depths, creating higher-percentage throws.

Before their Week 11 bye, almost half of the Rams' games will be against a defensive opponent with a top-10 rank in pressure rate or passing yards allowed. I still see them as a contender, but need to make a couple of adjustments. And with Kyren Williams and Blake Corum hitting season-highs in target rates, their involvement as receivers should continue to pick up until the primary options are healthy.

Now, contrast our level of confidence in a 1-2 team with an undefeated franchise.

Kyler Murray with a rocket to Jordan Addison for the TD 🚀@MINvsTB on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/VaM63tFsfW

— NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026

Granted, Justin Jefferson left early in the first quarter. But I'd give a mixed review of Kyler Murray's return. Head coach Todd Bowles blitzed Murray on 41.2% of his dropbacks. The Vikings line kept him clean for more than 2.5 seconds on over half of his pressures. But even when left to his own devices, Murray was 13 of 22 for 126 yards and an interception. At a 22.7% success rate, he was worse than Carson Wentz. But looking at his options, I can understand why.

  • Jordan Addison: 36.0% (Target Rate), 19.4 (aDOT)

  • Aaron Jones: 24.0%, -2.0

  • T.J. Hockenson: 16.0%, 8.8

  • Jauan Jennings: 8.0%, 10.5

Without a route runner like Jettas on the field, it was all or nothing for Murray. Despite Jennings running from the slot on 58.1% of his routes or Hockenson running a route on 73.5% of Murray's dropbacks, neither could earn more than five looks. Even worse, only half of them were catchable.

Luckily, the Vikings defense has the second-highest sack rate while allowing the third-fewest yards per drive. Murray has time to figure out his personnel. And games against the Dolphins and Saints before their bye are the right environment for "in-season tests." But without an intermediate option, we'll need to see more of Minnesota's WR2 to keep the Vikings atop the NFC North.

However, for the Texans, there are multiple factors at play keeping their win total at zero.

"CJ Stroud needs to play better"

Simple stunt brings immediate pressure up the middle, rolls right, delivers a perfect ball on the run while being hit. Two wrs scramble to same area and ball is dropped. lmao

2026 Texans offense in a nutshell pic.twitter.com/Bb9AHSIyQw

— Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) September 28, 2026

Honestly, the play above is a solid encapsulation of their season. The worst part is that the same post-snap issue plagued C.J. Stroud in '25. But he has fewer answers this time. 

  • Time to Pressure: 2.6 (2026), 2.5 (2025)

  • Average Time to Throw (when pressured): 3.3, 3.3

  • Pressure-to-Sack Rate: 19.6%, 13.4%

Houston's offensive line has broken down in less than 2.5 seconds on 54.9% of Stroud's dropbacks. Last season, one of Nico Collins, Dalton Schultz or Jayden Higgins would be there to support their QB. Injuries have removed two of them. But "replacing" them with Xavier Hutchinson, Jared Wayne and Foster Moreau has benefited Houston about as much as you can expect.

Nico Collins' return would give the Texans' passing a much-needed boost. But games against potent offenses like the Cowboys and Jaguars over their next four will remind us why slow starts can be death knells for teams with playoff aspirations.

It's not run vs. pass, it's shotgun vs. under center

If you missed the offseason debates, how offense could get back to generating explosives was a frequent topic. The defensive meta from six years ago that shut down big plays had shown some cracks. Progressive playcallers were finding ways around it. But even today, some of the old methods still work.

Christian McCaffrey just carried the Cardinals defense on his back! pic.twitter.com/O24aOAjDtw

— OurSF49ers (@OurSf49ers) September 27, 2026

Now, I know what you're thinking. All of the talk harped on QBs needing to be under center. That's how we get the chunk gains. Don't worry. We'll get to that. But offenses have two components, right? An aerial attack and a ground game. One can't exist without the other. However, to create more efficient runs, operating from shotgun can be the more optimal approach. 

I snagged the last five years of data and did a quick comparison between the pre-snap formations on rushing plays. Yes, on the surface, rushes from shotgun are better. But my use of "can be" a bit ago and the small margins for two of the three metrics emphasize the subtext: it depends.

Downhill rushers like Derrick Henry can use the runway for picking up speed. But when vision and agility are required, shotgun runners are (slightly) more effective. In short, having an RB or a platoon of them to add flexibility to your game plan takes pressure off your QB. But then, they need to pull their weight when the defense gives them the right look.

HC Ben Johnson had the Eagles' defense on skates for most of the night. Kyle Monangai had a 75.0% rushing success rate on his shotgun runs. D'Andre Swift was averaging 4.5 YPC. But look at Case Keenum's position before the TD pass to Kalif Raymond:

KALIF RAYMOND TO THE HOUSE

📺: ESPN pic.twitter.com/JYrzzQ1Ol0

— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) September 29, 2026

Of course, this is one rep from a single team with one of the best schemers in the league. Even with a backup QB, we'd expect a good play or two. Besides, Keenum threw a TD to Luther Burden III from shotgun earlier in the same game. But if you look at a larger sample, the choice is clear.

Passing efficiency increases when playing from under center. I used only EPA per play here, but CPOE and TD rate tell the same story.

Actually, let's go back to MNF for a quick sanity check.

  • (Keenum) Passing Success Rate: 85.7% (Under Center), 40.0% (Shotgun)

  • EPA per Dropback: 0.80, -0.32

  • Completion Rate: 92.9%, 55.0%

Keenum didn't cause a turnover or take a sack to influence the EPA values, and he threw a TD from either formation. It's about as clean of a single-game comparison as they come. And the answer is the same. But spinning it forward to the rest of the season, let's look at what this means for us.

  • Shotgun Run Rate: 32.8% (2026), 46.5% (2021-2025 Avg.)

  • Under-Center Passing Rate: 22.8%, 16.9%

We're living in an under-center world. Teams are foregoing shotgun snaps for both pass and run plays at a higher clip than in the past five years. Remember, the efficiency gaps for rushing from either formation were small, but noticeable. Accordingly, finding offenses that are trying to take advantage of these edges should be worth our time.

I pulled the rates of teams that are pulling both levers when sequencing plays. Truth be told, I'm not surprised to see Cleveland on the list. We liked HC Todd Monken when he was calling plays for Lamar Jackson. And Deshaun Watson has been, at worst, a practical fantasy streamer the past two weeks.

Regardless, finding teams that are leaning into these tendencies can net you viable starts. Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion should be mid-tier fantasy trade candidates. After Sunday afternoon, checking to see if a manager with George Pickens wants to sell low has its merits. Integrating these concepts is how offenses are looking to score in 2026. So, as fantasy managers, buying into offenses that are applying them should be our top priority.

Progress isn't linear

You've heard me say it before, but it bears repeating. Football isn't just about reps. There's a mental component that takes time to click for each player. So, assuming we "know" the extent of a receiver's capabilities based on draft capital or prior results can lead us astray at times (see Washington, Parker).

For instance, let's revisit Kalif Raymond's big night against Philadelphia.

  • Route Rate: 74.3%

  • Target Share: 20.6%

  • Air Yard Share: 24.3%

On the one hand, Raymond racked up 45.6% of his MNF yardage total on his touchdown catch-and-run. It'd be easy to dismiss a big play as a fluke. But the 32-year-old former UDFA has run just four fewer routes than Luther Burden III and only two targets behind the second-year receiver. Zooming in further, we can see how integrated Raymond is within this passing game.

  • Snap Share (w/ two or more TEs on the field): 38.7% (Raymond), 31.1% (Burden)

  • Slot Rate: 36.6%, 24.2%

  • Target Share: 11.1%, 13.9%

Burden isn't the only one affected here, too. With Raymond hoarding the interior and shallow looks (7.2-yard aDOT), Colston Loveland's opportunities have taken a hit. We have a fourth mouth to feed on the 19th-ranked offense in PROE. Lowering expectations for everyone, even with a reasonable schedule (Jets, Packers, Falcons and Patriots), should be our approach with the target tree expanding.

Finally, let's look at a case where the volume has condensed.

That's 3️⃣ TDs for Gibbs! Lions take the lead!@NYJvsDET on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/GKazqFPYdS

— NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026

Elite fantasy production sits at the intersection of talent and situation. To be clear, there was no question about Jahmyr Gibbs' talent. Since entering the league, only De'Von Achane has a higher explosive play rate. But after working alongside David Montgomery for years, Gibbs' usage matches his draft-price tag.

  • Rush Rate: 87.8% (2026), 40.4%

  • Target Share: 19.4%, 16.7%

  • Goal-line Touch Rate: 100.0%, 44.3%

Drafters with the 1.01, this is the scenario you needed. Isiah Pacheco is on IR until early December. Sione Vaki and Jacob Saylors have combined for nine snaps and nine carries. It's Gibbs time, all the time. Even better for fantasy managers, Detroit's defense will likely keep them in attack mode every week.

  • Yards per Drive Allowed: 2nd-most 

  • Touchdowns Surrendered: Most

  • Turnover Rate: T-2nd lowest

Before you ask, no, don't try to trade for Gibbs. There are better ways to find yourself getting dragged on social media. But keying in on the other beneficiaries would net you potential starters down the line. 

Sam LaPorta has one top-12 finish despite running a route on 86% of Jared Goff's dropbacks. Jameson Williams keeps making plays, but his highlights haven't translated to the box score yet. Marveling at players, even those not on our rosters, is a natural part of football. But finding ways to leverage their ecosystems for our gain is how we stay ahead of our leaguemates.

item.title: NFL Survivor contest picks, predictions, advice, strategy: My favorite Week 4 selections
item.description: Matt Russell runs through his Week 4 NFL Survivor pool plays, giving his favorite picks to help you advance.
item.content:encoded:
This season, there are two types of survivors in NFL Survivor contests:

  • Those who used the 49ers in Week 2

  • Those who didn’t and somehow survived anyway

So, when Week 3 came about, two road teams were among the popular choices, since, by implied win probability derived by the moneyline, the Chiefs and Seahawks were highly likely to win. 

As we see from the distribution numbers from Circa Sports’ massive Survivor contest, one made it out alive, the other didn’t:

We had the Chiefs among our top-three recommendations, but left the Seahawks out of the mix, and, sure enough, many of those wanting to save Kansas City, and who’d already used the 49ers, got washed away in the nor’easter. 

The Chiefs were the most popular selection so there wasn’t full-scale carnage in Week 3, and about a quarter of the original entrants in your pool should still be hanging around. 

Here is my Week 4 survivor pool analysis.

The number of remaining participants in your pool also changes the calculus when it comes to strategy. After all, the fewer the entrants, the less conceptual risk is necessary each week. 

Each week (until we’ve exhausted all reasonable paths of survival), we look at the Survivor Contest landscape, and the best options available, while understanding that it matters who you’ve already taken, and what you might be giving up by burning a team that week.

Week 4 moneylines

How likely is a team to win and you'll advance? The betting market provides the answer to that each week with the moneyline, which we can convert to an implied win probability.

Market power ratings

It's not as simple as picking the team most likely to win, because once you use that team, you can't use it again. What is simple is that if you're going to make it through the 18-week season, then you need to use 18 teams. That means, at some point, you'll be trusting the 18th-best team in the NFL — an unnerving thought. 

Here's a list of the current top 18 teams (with help from the betting market), and an estimation of their value to the point spread: 

  • Rams: 19.7

  • Bills: 18.9

  • Ravens: 18.6

  • Seahawks: 17.3

  • Chiefs: 17.3

  • 49ers: 16.7

  • Bengals: 16.7

  • Broncos: 16.2

  • Texans: 16.2

  • Jaguars: 16.2

  • Lions: 15.7

  • Cowboys: 15.4

  • Eagles: 14.9

  • Vikings: 14.9

  • Packers: 13.5

  • Colts: 13.2

  • Bears: 12.2

Picking the most likely team to win each week, or the highest available team on this list above, means that you're giving up the opportunity to use it later, and while every week is technically created equal, trusting a team in September is nerve-wracking, but doing so at some point in December is real tension. 

Week 4's top choices

As we look at the best options for Week 4 and onward, we'll be factoring in the decision tree that will sprout from that pick. The implied probability derived from the moneyline should answer any questions about why the favorite should win, but the nuance is found in what you're giving up by using it now and not later (with a projected point spread projection for those matchups). 

Vikings (85.1%) over Dolphins 

At 0-3, the Dolphins have been the No. 1 fade for Survivor players the last two weeks, on the road at San Francisco and at home versus the Chiefs. Those teams are playoff regulars, while the Vikings came into the season as the fourth betting choice to win the NFC North. 

Without De’Von Achane, Malik Willis will have to deal with Brian Flores’ defense without his most dangerous weapon. The Dolphins defense has shown some modest improvement, but now that he’s played a full game, Kyler Murray should be more comfortable against them than he was last week in Tampa Bay. Plus, if there’s the dreaded quarterback injury, Carson Wentz has already seen action this season.

Estimated Availability: 99.4%

What you’re giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 12 vs. Falcons (MIN -6.5)

  • Week 13 vs. Panthers (MIN -6.5)

  • Week 16 vs. Commanders (MIN -6)

With the only other times where the Vikings are a reasonable option all in games with a projected line under a full touchdown, it’s clear that this is one of those situations where it’s time to use a borderline top-18 team if you’re going to use them at all.

Ravens (85.8%) over Titans 

In 2024, the Packers and Eagles opened the season in Brazil — the first NFL game played in South America, and a 10-hour flight. 

Because that game was played on a Friday, each of them had more than a week to rest and readjust after the long road trip, but neither of them played particularly well in Week 2. In Green Bay, Jordan Love got hurt, and the Packers barely got past the Anthony Richardson-led Colts. In Philadelphia, the Eagles were beaten in the final minute by Kirk Cousins and the Falcons on a Monday night. 

The Ravens (and Cowboys) only have six days before they’re expected to play well and be trusted to win for those selecting them in Survivor. Luckily, Baltimore is playing the Titans, who’ve beaten one quarterback (Kyler Murray) that’s currently starting in the NFL since a Week 12 win over the Texans in 2024. 

Estimated Availability: 99.1%

What you’re giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 10 vs. Chargers (BAL -7.5)

  • Week 14 vs. Buccaneers (BAL -7.5)

  • Week 16 vs. Browns (BAL -11)

The Chargers and Buccaneers could have their act together by Week 10 and Week 14, respectively. 

Next to the Dolphins, the Titans set up as weekly whipping boys and one of the first looks to fade, but in Week 16 their opponent is the Raiders. There is the Lions, who host the Giants in Week 16, and New York’s starting quarterback is already lost for the season.

Seahawks (74.9%) over Chargers 

Every week, the Chargers get more desperate for a win, but are they capable of actually not shooting themselves in the metaphorical foot like they did on repeat in Buffalo? 

A trip to Seattle against an ornery team coming off a loss, who hasn’t played in front of the 12s since Sept. 9, doesn’t seem like a recipe for a breakthrough. 

Estimated Availability: 98.3%

What you’re giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 9 vs. Cardinals (SEA -8.5)

  • Week 14 vs. Giants (SEA -10.5)

By point spread, there are two better times to use the Seahawks. Seattle’s next four opponents are legitimate playoff teams, but at least it might create a scenario where their urgency will be cranked all the way up. On top of that, we just saw the Hawks win at Arizona with Drew Lock at the helm. 

After a look at the other Week 9 matchups, I’d happily take my chances with Seattle. You just have to make it that far first.

item.description: Being undefeated has its perks
item.content:encoded:
The Las Vegas Raiders are one of the top stories in the NFL after they have started 3-0 to begin this season. The perfect stats changes and affects a lot of things about this team moving forward. Let’s discuss:

Trade talk:

There was a lot of speculation the Raiders could potentially revisit the idea of trading star defensive end Maxx Crosby before the November 10 deadline. But if the Raiders stay in the playoff hunt they likely will not be interested in weakening this roster. In fact, the Raiders may be deadline buyers rather than sellers.

Award talk:

Klint Kubiak for Coach of the Year? Kirk Cousins for MVP? Zeke Masses for Defensive Rookie of the Year? Brock Bowers for Offensive Player of the Year? Yes, all of it.

Raider Nation, take the conversation everywhere!

The SB Nation app keeps you connected to fellow Raiders fans before, during and after every game.

  • Join the live game-day chat
  • Enjoy fewer ads
  • Move seamlessly between communities and conversations
  • Comment and post faster

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Playoff-chase cushion:

The Raiders are entering a tough eight-week stretch. They are built to survive it, even if they don’t have a winning record in the stretch. Say, Las Vegas wins three of the next eight games. They’d still be 6-5 and very likely still in the playoff hunt heading into the stretch run. They’ve built themselves a nice cushion.

Mendoza timeline:

Fernando Mendoza, you remember, right? The question of when he will become the Raiders’ starting quarterback has long been the topic surrounding the team. Now, with the team undefeated and Cousins playing great football, the Mendoza talk is on the backburner. If the Raiders keep winning and Cousins stays a big reason why, a change is extremely unlikely.

Draft order:

Raiders fans are used to this team picking high. That may not the case in 2027. So, that could change the path for a top wide receiver. Jeremiah Smith and Charlie Becker may require a trade-up scenario if the Raiders covet either of them.

Flexed games:

The Raiders weren’t assigned any prime-time games when the schedule was released in May. That could change soon. If the Raiders keep winning, they could get flexed into a night game. A game to keep an eye on is the November 8 gamee at the San Francisco 49ers possibly getting bumped up to Sunday Night Football.

Assistant coach could be coveted:

Every January, teams like to pluck assistants from winning teams. That could happen with Kubiak’s staff. Could Rob Leonard get some head-coaching consideration after just one year a defensive coordinator? Yes, I could see him getting some interviews, at least.

See, winning changes everything.

item.title: Falcons sign LB Brian Asamoah
item.description: The Falcons add special teams help ahead of Monday Night Football.
item.content:encoded:
With Atlanta’s special teams off to a forgettable start to the 2026 season, they’ve added a veteran linebacker to hopefully help their coverage and return units. That would be former Viking and Bengal Brian Asamoah.

Asamoah, 26, had a solid rookie season as a defender in limited opportunities but has been a complete non-factor on that side of the ball in three seasons since, piling up just 70 total snaps on D from 2023 to 2025. Over that same span, he has nearly 600 special teams snaps and has been a solid tackler and useful blocker who was instrumental in paving the way for a 98 yard Charlie Jones kickoff return touchdown for the Bengals last year. He’ll likely be active on gameday for those attributes alone, as the Falcons are quite stacked at linebacker—Divine Deablo, Harold Perkins Jr., and Kendal Daniels are all off to strong starts, and Josh Woods is a capable reserve—and Asamoah has not played well there since 2022.

It’s not difficult to figure out why the Falcons felt the need to make a move. While Brian Robinson is a capable kick returner and Zachariah Branch a potentially dynamic punt returner, both have had early miscues that overshadowed the inconsistent blocking they’ve gotten thus far. Things have been worrying in coverage, as well, as the Falcons have avoided any catastrophic mistakes but also have nine missed tackles through just three games, led by Mike Ford with three. While Asamoah never became the starting-caliber linebacker the Vikings were hoping to get when they drafted him in the third round, there’s little question he can be a sure tackler and blocker on teams.

Give him a warm welcome, if you would, and we’ll see if he’s active for Monday Night Football.

item.title: 2 good things we learned about the Cowboys after Week 3 loss
item.description: What did you learn about the Cowboys in Week 3?
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys came out strong against the Baltimore Ravens in Brazil by building an early lead, and even after falling behind, came back to almost win it. Even with the loss, here are two good things we learned in Rio.

Jaishawn Barham is an absolute stud

One of the biggest bright spots for the Cowboys in their loss to the Ravens was the play of linebacker Jaishawn Barham. He ended up with seven tackles with four being solo, and two of them were for a loss. When the Cowboys put together a goal line stand against the Ravens in the fourth quarter, Barham was at his best by combining on two consecutive tackles and then putting up a solo stop on Derrick Henry for a three-yard loss on 4th and goal from the one-yard line.

Barham also stopped Henry along with Caleb Downs on a 4th and 1 early in the game. He was very decisive and played downhill all game long, which is exactly what you want from a middle linebacker. After struggling in his first game as a rookie against the New York Giants, Barham has been lights out for two consecutive weeks. He is settling in just fine, and he’s becoming one of the most important players on defense for Dallas.

The Cowboys found balance in their offensive attack

In the first two games, the Cowboys struggled to get the run game going. Williams only had 71 yards on 24 carries in the first two weeks, and as a team, they were only averaging 67.5 yards per game. Against the Ravens, Williams had 98 yards on 19 carries, and the team ran for 148 yards total.

Prescott was able to hook up with CeeDee Lamb seven times for 112 yards. After only amassing 68 yards in the first two weeks, George Pickens hauled in seven passes for 82 yards with four of them moving the chains for first downs. This is the type of balance that the Cowboys need to keep opposing defenses honest so that they can pick them apart. They’ll need more of that in this next stretch of winnable games as they try to improve on their 1-2 record.

item.title: The Packers’ offensive line renovation is wild and unprecedented
item.description: We’re living through unprecedented Packers moves.
item.content:encoded:
I can’t talk about the Packers’ offensive line renovations without using hyperbolic language.

You generally want to avoid descriptors  like “desperate” and “panicked” and “last-ditch attempt to save their season and their jobs,” when trying to write anything resembling sober, reasoned analysis of a team. For one thing, it’s rarely that serious. For another, it paints you as the kind of person who can’t be trusted to react appropriately to things.

But seriously, how else would you describe what the Packers have done over the past few days? After a truly apocalyptic start to the year, the Packers have signed three different replacement offensive linemen, raiding the Cowboys’ practice squad for Laken Tomlinson and picking up Mekhi Becton and Kevin Zeitler off the street.

That’s a flurry of activity virtually unprecedented in the corners of Packers history I’m aware of. I’ve been writing about this team in some format for about 20 years now and was a fan for long before that, and I can’t recall any kind of in-season renovation at a position group like we’re seeing now.

The Packers have added notable in-season free agents before, but it’s usually one at a time. They’ve tried late-career mercenary signings with guys like Snacks Harrison and Whitney Mercilus. They added Cedric Benson just before the start of the 2012 season to fix a moribund running back room. The most famous example of all is probably Andre Rison, claimed off of waivers late in the 1996 season.

But those are all one-off moves. This is entirely different.

Tomlinson, Becton, and Zeitler could all start for the Packers. Two of the three, in some combination, will probably be starting sooner than later. Given how the injury bug has infected the Packers’ offensive line, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see all of them in the starting lineup at some point.

That’s not normal! You don’t just sign three new starting offensive linemen during the season! It’d be noteworthy enough to be remarkable had they done it in the offseason, but we’re sitting here in late September discussing three new linemen joining the team. That’s bananas!

We can only speculate as to what caused the sudden flurry of activity. The need for help was obvious to anyone with eyes, but neither Brian Gutekunst or Matt LaFleur seemed overly inclined to do anything about it for the first three weeks. We watched Donovan Jennings get shoved up and down the field for most of two weeks before Lafleur even tried Jager Burton at left guard, for goodness sake, and prior to the spending spree of the last few days, Brian Gutekunst’s big move was signing Cordell Volson to the practice squad.

Did Ed Policy throw a fit? Did he give the recently extended pair of Gutekunst and LaFleur a “fix it or you’re fired” ultimatum? It’s hard not to conclude something happened behind closed doors, because we’ve all lived through a very un-Packers-like few days since they farted out an embarrassing home loss to the Falcons on Thursday Night Football.

Whether or not these moves end up helping is anybody’s guess, but we’re certainly going to find out. But whether it works or not, the Packers are making unprecedented moves. Who knows what caused it, but we can’t avoid the words that accurately describe what it is. It’s desperate, it’s more than a little panicky, and it could still all be for naught.

item.title: The Chiefs are using play action as well as anyone in the NFL
item.description: Kansas City is making life easier on its quarterback this year.
item.content:encoded:
Coming into the season, the conversation about the Kansas City Chiefs‘ offense focused on what would change.

They ran into a wall with the previous version of the offense and needed to make changes. This offseason, their only meaningful addition was signing running back Kenneth Walker. Signing a good running back was the easiest way for the Chiefs to boost their offense. They couldn’t generate explosive runs last year and got nothing from their running backs. Any semblance of a run game would improve the offense.

Another benefit of having Walker is that the improved run game has opened up the Chiefs’ play-action calls, which have been wildly successful this year.

According to Next Gen Stats, Mahomes has had 36 dropbacks on play action this year. On those plays, he has a 71% completion rate, 348 passing yards, 3 TDs, and 1 interception, with a 69% success rate. He has thrown 11 passes over 20 yards. That is absurd efficiency that easily tops the NFL.

So, what is driving Mahomes’s success with play action? Let’s dive into some of his best plays of the year:

Film Review

One of the best ways to get Mahomes going is to get him on the run, and the bootleg lets him do that.

Kansas City has done a good job protecting the backside of the bootleg to keep Mahomes clean, and he can make any throw on the run.

Getting Rashee Rice to the middle of the field is how he’ll succeed, and play action has helped. The Chiefs can get him on crossers. Condensing the formation means he doesn’t have to beat press, and he can get a leverage advantage. He can stay off contact, and Mahomes can throw a fastball to get Rice going in space.

Moving to this style of offense seems to have unlocked something in tight end Travis Kelce. He’s been great running routes and finding soft spots, but even deeper downfield than before. He also benefits from being closer to the line of scrimmage more, where he can get free releases and find soft spots between linebackers.

Condensing the formation makes it hard for teams to play man coverage against you, and the Chiefs have won the leverage advantage every week with their passing concepts.

This is one of the best corner-route throws you’ll ever see. Mahomes short rolls, runs himself into the defensive lineman’s vision, and throws a fade-away on a 24-yard downfield throw. It’s pristine accuracy and touch. Mahomes’s accuracy on these downfield throws off play action has been insane. He can hit any throw on the field from any angle.

Mahomes can hit Rice with a fastball, but he can also lob it up and still hit him. As I mentioned above, Mahomes’ touch has been insane this year. Every downfield pass hits a player in stride, and the ball is never in conflict. He’s making it very easy on his receivers to make plays.

The Bottom Line

When I watched these clips, the comparison for how Mahomes is playing right now was Matthew Stafford last year with the Los Angeles Rams. Stafford was unbelievable using play action last year, and it won him an MVP. He could hit any blade of grass with either a fastball or touch. He had great chemistry with everyone.

Mahomes has that right now, but he also has more mobility than Stafford did. The Chiefs can boot Mahomes more and get him on the run, which puts even more stress on a defense. They can change the angles and launch points and create misdirection.

It’s also a great fit with the Chiefs’ current personnel. Rashee Rice and Travis Kelce need free releases to be successful, and going under center more often helps you do that. Walker and Emmett Johnson are good checkdown guys that can create in the passing game. Thornton does a good job on the vertical clearout routes that are essential to opening up space.

The one thing missing is a receiver who can beat press and play on the outside. That’s what the Chiefs are asking Xavier Worthy to do right now, and he’s just not good at that. It’s been true for three years now. If they can improve that spot at the trade deadline, the Chiefs’ offense could become the best in the league.

The New York Jets are playing pretty well this year and already have three first-round picks next year, so I doubt No. 1 receiver Garrett Wilson becomes available. The guys who might become available are guys like Marvin Harrison Jr. of the Arizona Cardinals, Brian Thomas Jr. of the Jacksonville Jaguars, or Jordan Addison of the Minnesota Vikings. Those are three guys whose teams aren’t going to pay and who might want some value. If any of those guys become available, I think the Chiefs should really look into it.

All three of those players haven’t been great in the NFL, but they would be an upgrade over Worthy. At the very least, that helps your offense. If you get lucky, you could tap into their upside, and they could become a long-term core piece. But even if that doesn’t happen, they would immediately improve the room.

The Chiefs’ picks are always going to be near the end of the rounds anyway, and they have an extra third-round pick this year. I think this would be a good year to get aggressive at wide receiver and see if you can find someone. If the Chiefs can find one more functional wide receiver, they could have the best offense in the NFL, with Mahomes, a great run game, and Kelce and Rice filling key roles. We’ll see if that receiver becomes available.

item.title: 5 Lions vs. Panthers thoughts after watching Carolina’s loss to Browns
item.description: 5 lessons we learned about Lions vs. Panthers from Carolina’s loss to the Cleveland Browns.
item.content:encoded:
To begin my scouting of the Detroit Lions’ next opponent, I like to watch their most recent game played. For the Carolina Panthers, that means checking in on their 21-18 loss to the Cleveland Browns in Week 3.

I took notes during the game, and here are my five biggest takeaways on what it may mean for Lions vs. Panthers, along with some data to support those observations.

The Panthers defense can get to the passer… but they have to get aggressive

Against the Browns, the Panthers posted a 38.5% pressure rate, but that dropped significantly when just rushing four. Here are their pressure rates in Week 3 with and without blitz:

  • Blitzing: 55.6% pressure rate (fourth highest), 2.76 seconds to pressure (29th)
  • No blitz: 33.3% pressure rate (10th), 2.93 seconds to pressure (22nd)

When the Panthers don’t send extra blitzers, they generate their pressure utilizing the speed of their edge rushers. Princely Umanmielen is second in pressures on the team, only trailing Jaelen Phillips, and his speed and bend were on display against Cleveland. But the Lions dealt with a pair of speed rushers last week against the Jets and held up very well.

That said, they’ve got some interior players with some pass rushing skills, including Derrick Brown (7.0 sacks last year). That could be the bigger threat against Detroit’s young interior.

Bryce Young’s arm talent is a problem

Man, Bryce Young is fun to watch when you’re only looking at arm talent. He can make any throw. And while the deep shots are what get most of the national attention, I’m impressed with the throws he can make on the perimeter in tight windows. Just look at his passing chart against the Browns and how he utilized every inch of the boundaries:

It takes a ton of arm talent to drive that ball all the way to the sidelines, and he is not afraid to do so.

He is also not afraid to air it out deep. He currently holds the longest intended air yards per pass attempt in the league (10.2) and leads the league in passes of 20+ air yards (17). The accuracy is a bit up and down, but there’s more good than bad there.

And while we’re on the topic of Young, his mobility is obviously something defenses need to be aware of. He can extend plays with his legs and his pocket presence is clearly improving. However, interestingly, he is much less inclined to run and scramble. Against the Browns, he passed up several opportunities for easy yards to try for the big play. For the season, he has attempted just three rushes for 16 yards and a touchdown.

Panthers’ standard run game struggled, but came alive late

For the season, the Panthers run game has been fairly ineffective. They rank 21st in DVOA, 23rd in EPA, and 23rd in success rate.

However, they do have the ability to wear teams down as the game continues. Against the Browns, Carolina had just 22 yards on 11 carries through three quarters. But in the final quarter, they ran the ball down Cleveland’s throat, rushing for 76 yards on just 12 carries (6.3 YPC).

With a pair of bruising backs in Chuba Hubbard (6-foot-1, 210) and AJ Dillon (6-foot, 247), they can wear you down—but they are not explosive. The Panthers’ longest run of the season is 24 yards by… Kenny Pickett. The running backs don’t have a run over 16 yards.

Detroit may need to defend all four downs

Panthers head coach Dave Canales is not afraid to get a little aggressive on fourth down. Twice in the first half against the Browns, Carolina opted to go for it near midfield. Here were the two opportunities:

  • 8:38 left in the second quarter: 0-0 tie, fourth-and-3 from the Browns’ 43-yard line
  • 3:40 left in the second quarter: 3-0 Browns, fourth-and-1 from the Panthers’ 40-yard line

The Panthers failed both attempts, and it immediately led to two Browns’ scoring drives and a 10-0 deficit. If Detroit can stand their ground on fourth down (Lions currently have stopped zero of three fourth down attempts), it could be a game-changer.

For the year, the Panthers are just 1-of-6 on fourth down. Last year, they attempted the second most fourth downs in the NFL (40), converting on 27 of them (67.5% conversion rate, fourth best).

Panthers run defense maybe better than advertised

If you look at the season-long stats for Carolina’s run defense, they look god awful. They’ve allowed an NFL-high 5.7 yards per carry, 193.3 rushing yards per game, and they rank 23rd in run defense DVOA.

However, I think three things are happening: the data is being swung by a terrible Week 1 performance against the Bears, they’re being disproportionately hurt by mobile quarterbacks, and they’ve also just made some clear progress.

Against Chicago, the Panthers allowed 291 rushing yards and 7.5 yards per carry. It was a truly awful performance, led by D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai, who combined for 224 yards and four touchdowns on 28 carries (8.0 YPC). The following week wasn’t great, but it was a marked improvement: allowing Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson to combine for 123 yards on 27 carries (4.6 YPC). Against the Browns, the Panthers allowed 132 rushing yards on 4.4 yards per carry—but Quinshon Judkins managed just 70 yards on 18 carries (3.9 YPC).

In total, of the 580 rushing yards the Panthers have allowed, 146 (over 25%) have come from quarterbacks. That won’t be an issue this week.

Particularly, when it came down to needing their defense to stop the run, they did. The Browns had an opportunity to put the game away late with a single first down clinching it. Despite facing a second-and-2, the Panthers were able to get three straight stops on runs to give the offense one more shot. That is reflected in their overall run success rate allowed (35.6%), which is actually ninth best in the NFL

Now, the Browns’ rushing attack (31st in DVOA) is way worse than the Bears (ninth) and Falcons (sixth), and the Lions have one of the best in the NFL (second). But I still think the early numbers are skewing a run defense that can hang.

item.title: Commanders QB Jayden Daniels to practice Wednesday after flying to London with team, still 'a chance' he plays vs. Colts in Week 4
item.description: The Commanders haven't yet ruled Daniels out for a Week 4 return.
item.content:encoded:
Injured quarterback Jayden Daniels traveled with the Washington Commanders to London and is set to participate in a “jog-through” in a limited capacity, head coach Dan Quinn shared with reporters Wednesday.

The Commanders will play the Indianapolis Colts in London on Sunday, just two weeks after Daniels suffered an elbow injury for the second time over the past two seasons.

Linebacker Frankie Luvu (groin) and tight end Chig Okonkwo (hamstring) were also expected to travel and practice this week after being sidelined with injuries.

Could Daniels return to play in Week 4?

Daniels suffered a dislocated elbow in his non-throwing arm in Week 2 and missed Sunday's win over the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. Backup Marcus Mariota started at quarterback in the 33-31 win.

The injury is to the same elbow that Daniels dislocated and re-injured last season. However, flying Daniels to London and having him available to practice indicates they’re not quite ready to rule him out for Sunday’s contest against the Colts.

Quinn confirmed as much to reporters Wednesday, saying that there is still “a chance” Daniels could play in Week 4, but “We’re not going to put him out there before he’s ready.”

Though the team never gave a specific timetable for Daniels’ return, the Commanders declined to place him on injured reserve, indicating that there's hope that he could return to the field in fewer than four weeks from his injury.

The injury knocked Daniels out of Washington's Week 2 loss to the Dallas Cowboys and initially raised fears of a long-term absence.

But Commanders general manager Adam Peters revealed last week that "surgery is not on the table." And NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Sunday that consultations with medical specialists concluded that Daniels is "expected back at three weeks or sooner."

A return to face the Colts would fall within that reported timeline, but is obviously far from certain as of Monday.

Washington is 1-2 following Sunday's upset win. The Commanders have a chance to build on that success with upcoming games against the Colts and Giants before the schedule gets tougher in Weeks 6-8 with games against the 49ers, Eagles and Rams. They'd certainly like to have Daniels back sooner rather than later.

Leon Chenal had neck surgery

Linebacker Leo Chenal, meanwhile, underwent season-ending neck surgery Monday morning. Quinn confirmed the news Monday, telling reporters that the procedure "went well."

Chenal sustained his neck injury on Sunday. He was placed on a stabilizing backboard and carted off the field vs. the Seahawks after taking contact to his head. He had movement in his extremities as he was carted off the field.

Chenal, 25, joined the Commanders from the Chiefs in the offseason and started at inside linebacker.

item.title: A look back at the history between the Saints and Falcons
item.description: How did it all start between these two rival teams?
item.content:encoded:
In Week 4, the New Orleans Saints will face their first NFC South opponent of the season when they host the Atlanta Falcons for a Monday Night Football showdown on Oct. 5 in the Caesars Superdome.

The Saints-Falcons rivalry dates back to Nov. 26, 1967, when New Orleans defeated Atlanta 27-24 at Tulane Stadium during the Saints’ inaugural season. Monday night will mark the 114th meeting between the two franchises, including one postseason matchup, with Atlanta holding a slim 58-56 edge in the all-time series.

Despite the long history between these two teams, they have faced each other just once in the playoffs. That meeting came on Dec. 28, 1991, when the Falcons defeated the Saints 27-20 in an NFC Wild Card matchup at the Louisiana Superdome. New Orleans entered the fourth quarter with a 20-17 lead, but Atlanta responded with 10 unanswered points, highlighted by a 61-yard touchdown pass from Chris Miller to Michael Haynes with 2:41 remaining to seal the victory.

While the 1991 playoff meeting remains the only postseason game between the two teams, there have been plenty of memorable moments throughout the rivalry. None, however, were more significant than the “Domecoming” game on Sept. 25, 2006. The Monday night matchup marked the Saints’ return to the Superdome following Hurricane Katrina and became one of the most iconic nights in franchise history.

Steve Gleason’s blocked punt, recovered by Curtis Deloatch in the end zone for a touchdown, provided one of the defining moments of the night as the Saints went on to defeat the Falcons 23-3.

Twenty years later, these longtime rivals will meet again under the bright lights of the Superdome as the NFL and New Orleans commemorates the anniversary of a game that meant far more than just football to the city and its fans.

Kickoff is at 7:15 p.m. CT and the game will be broadcast on ESPN with Joe Buck (play-by-play), Troy Aikman (color analyst) and Laura Rutledge and Lisa Salters (sideline)

item.title: Patriots confident in bounce-back skills heading into Bills matchup
item.description: The Patriots are entering Week 4 off a blowout loss in Jacksonville.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots had their proverbial doors blown off in Week 3 by the Jacksonville Jaguars, and are now heading into a pivotal division battle with the Buffalo Bills facing more questions than answers. Standing above all of them is a simple one: how will they respond?

Despite now being 1-2 and coming off the worst loss of the Mike Vrabel era, there is optimism for a bounce-back.

“I have a lot of faith and confidence in everybody that is here. That is why they’re here,” said Vrabel himself when talking to the media on Monday. “We have to continue to prepare and work with one another. The answers are here. The answers are in this building. We just have to do it much more consistently and continue to find ways to do it together.”

The biggest issue for the Patriots through three weeks has been their inability to finish drives, with Drake Maye the main culprit. The third-year quarterback has thrown six interceptions to just one touchdown and also lost a fumble.

Getting Maye back on track has to be the team’s top priority right now. However, the pressure will not just be on him, but the rest of the team as well come Sunday.

The 35-6 defeat in Jacksonville, after all, was a comprehensive one: offense, defense and special teams all failed to play up to their capabilities.

“It’s definitely a bounce-back week when it comes down to it,” said cornerback and team captain Marcus Jones. “It definitely challenges the situation of our leadership, captains and everything. We know what we have in the locker room and when it comes down to it, we have to stick together. We all know that. So, we are going to get back to practice, do the things that we need to do, and then go from there.”

Doing all that is easier said than done, especially with a game against the unbeaten Bills coming up. However, hope, or in this case a belief in the program, dies last in the New England locker room.

“I love this group,” added linebacker Christian Elliss. “We have a lot of playmakers. We have a lot of guys that have been in this position before. We’ll see. At the end of the day, you have to lace them up again and see what happens. But I know we’re going to respond.”

item.title: Packers reportedly sign guard Kevin Zeitler, completely overhauling offensive line after poor start
item.description: The Packers are already making big changes on their offensive line.
item.content:encoded:
Just three weeks into the 2026 regular season, the Green Bay Packers are already making big changes. The team continued its offensive-line overhaul Wednesday, reportedly agreeing to a deal with veteran guard Kevin Zeitler, per ESPN.

Zeitler, 36, spent last season with the Tennessee Titans, starting all 16 games in which he played. He rated out well by Pro Football Focus' metrics, ranking as the 13th best guard in football last season.

More offensive line help; Veteran guard Kevin Zeitler, who has played 14 NFL seasons, is signing a one-year deal with the Green Bay Packers, per sources. This week, the Packers now have added veteran offensive linemen Zeitler, Laken Tomlinson and Mekhi Becton. pic.twitter.com/k6Sh57nk69

— Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) September 30, 2026

While the move is notable, it takes on far more importance with context. With the signing, the Packers have now signed three veteran offensive lineman ahead of Week 4. The team signed guard Laken Tomlinson on Saturday and Mekhi Becton on Monday. After going through the entire offseason with one group, the Packers appear to be pivoting in a major way at the position after just three weeks.

There are some key reasons the team is aggressively looking for upgrades on the offensive line. Through three games, the Packers have the worst rushing output of any team. Green Bay has rushed for just 146 yards, nearly 100 fewer than the next closest team. Some of that is due to personnel. The Packers have not found a suitable replacement for starter Josh Jacobs, who is on the commissioner's exempt list after an offseason arrest.

But the majority of the fault lies with the line, which — in addition to producing awful rushing numbers — hasn't played well in the pass game, either. The Packers had the worst pass protection metrics of any team after their Week 3 game, per PFF. The team had also allowed 51 pressures following that contest, an extremely high figure.

Those struggles have affected every part of the offense. The Packers can't win on run plays, leading to their running backs being stopped immediately. When the team tries to pass, defenders are getting into the backfield too quickly, putting pressure on quarterback Jordan Love and resulting in him taking too many hits, even when he releases the ball.

All of that has added up to the team ranking 22nd in points per game this season.

While the Packers at least seem aware of the issue, it's unclear whether their signings will be capable of turning things around. The fact that the trio were still available this deep into the season suggests other NFL teams were skeptical of all three players, even though Zeitler graded out well last season.

Getting the offense back on track would go a long way toward the Packers salvaging their season. At 1-2, the team is already at the bottom of the NFC North. There's still plenty of time to turn that around, but early returns haven't been promising.

It's possible the team's signings will right the ship. It's also possible that it's already too little, too late for Green Bay, which should have addressed its line in the offseason if it wanted to see significant improvement at the position.

item.title: Bills penalties even worse than you likely thought against the Chargers
item.description: It was a very rough day for the Bills when it comes to yellow laundry
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills were heavily favored to beat the Los Angeles Chargers and while they did win, it was a much bigger ordeal than anyone thought it would be. The five turnovers were a pretty big deal, but the chatter on penalties has been nearly as loud this week. That’s 100% valid too with the Bills putting up near-record numbers when it comes to my proprietary penalty rating stat.

Note: As a heads up for this week, I dedicated my film and media creation time to a second penalty article on the controversial roughing the passer calls this weekend. Keep an eye out for that.

Standard and Advanced Metrics

Penalty Counts

Right off the bat this is bad. Not near-historic as the headline suggests, but still very bad. From this perspective, the Chargers didn’t have a great game either, landing firmly on average. Though again, average was a darn sight better than where the Bills were.

Penalty Yards

The assessed yards plays out about as you’d expect based on count, but it’s always the true yards where things start getting interesting in my opinion. Buffalo made it very interesting impacting/negating 47 yards beyond the assessed. Buffalo negated almost as many yards as the Chargers had assessed.

Penalty Harm

Los Angeles Chargers

When it’s all said and done though, per my Harm metric the Chargers had an alright day with 7.6 Harm total, decently below our “bad day” line of 10.0 Harm. In fact the largest spike is the 2 for Cole Strange’s count of false start flags. Every year I debate the utility of having the count of the penalty in the graph per player, and every year at least one person shows me why we need it.

There’s really very little interesting to see here with Joe Alt’s offensive holding negating a nine-yard scramble by Justin Herbert being the most captivating tale by itself. If you’re into formulas and are new to this metric or forgot how it works, all yards are counted as 0.1 Harm. For Alt that’s 10 yards for the assessed and nine yards negated for 19 yards total or 1.9 Harm.

The biggest impediment to their success was perhaps two false starts called with only a single play between them in the third quarter. The first one occurred on 2nd & goal at the one-yard line. Now 2nd & 6, Los Angeles tried a pass which was incomplete. And then another false start to force 3rd & 11. Rather than two or perhaps three goal line runs which likely yield a touchdown, the Chargers settled for a field goal.

Buffalo Bills

Dawson Knox’s offensive holding singlehandedly had higher Harm than the Chargers’ entire output for the day. Whereas yards are counted as 0.1 Harm, downs and points are all counted as 1.0 Harm for each one.

In Knox’s case, his flag called back a Ray Davis touchdown or 7.0 points/Harm alone. The flag itself was 10 yards and also negated 14 yards of Davis’ 43 yard run. Potentially the most exciting play of the game tarnished. On the plus side, the play was on fourth down and the holding occurred after the first was gained, which Buffalo was able to keep.

Christian Benford’s defensive holding flag was another major screw up. It gave up a free down in addition to the five assessed yards. It also wiped out an interception. Turnovers are treated as negating four downs of opportunity for your own team. Even in a three-and-out situation, the punt can drastically alter field position, hence the count of four downs lost.

The Bills had a total of 26.5 Harm, not even in the same zip code as our 10.0 bad day threshold. It wasn’t the worst game since I’ve made the stat. That honors goes to the 2020 game against the Denver Broncos, that saw three touchdowns negated. But it wasn’t too far off from that record of 33.2 Harm either.

A reminder that the Rousseau flag will be covered in detail in a separate article, but as a teaser I’m not a fan of that one being called. Overall, I felt the flags were warranted and the repeated attempts to hand over the game due to mistakes were genuine misfires by the Bills.

item.title: Steelers Week 4 power rankings roundup
item.description: Pittsburgh Steelers Week 4 power rankings roundup.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers offense came to life on Sunday, as they defeated the Cincinnati Bengals 30-27 at Acrisure Stadium. The same offense that looked largely lifeless through the first two weeks, scoring only 16 points, showed great improvement. With rookie Max Iheanachor and veteran Brock Hoffman now starting on the right side of the offensive line, the Steelers seem to have more freedom running the ball, and Aaron Rodgers seems to have more time to get rid of the ball to his receivers.

Let’s take a look at various media outlets to see how much of a bump the Steelers got in the rankings after handing the Bengals their first loss of 2026.

FOX Sports: No.14  (No. 21 Last Week)

“Aaron Rodgers going throw-for-throw with Joe Burrow at his age, and after his ugly start to the season, wasn’t on anybody’s Bingo card. He even dusted off DK Metcalf, his forgotten No. 1 receiver, and RB Jaylen Warren had a big game with Rico Dowdle out. Beating the Bengals was huge, surprising (at least to me), and deserving of a big jump, even if none of this is exactly how head coach Mike McCarthy drew it up. It was the first sign of life from the Steelers’ stagnant offense. There are no defensive juggernauts in the next five weeks before their bye week, so they’ve got a chance to go on a run if they can keep the scoring up.” – Ralph Vacchiano

The Athletic: No.14  (Last Week No.21)

“It’s been a big season already for NFL lip-readers. Aaron Rodgers gave them a clip to dissect Sunday in which he was either very mad at Michael Pittman Jr. after a dropped pass, very mad about the overall state of the Steelers offense or just rehearsing material for his next appearance on “The Pat McAfee Show.” It’s tough to tell with Rodgers, who has Pittsburgh in a crowded race in the AFC North despite being beaten by six drops (the third most in the league). He hasn’t been great either, though. He’s 33rd in EPA per dropback (minus-0.26).“ – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall

CBS Sports: No.13 (Last Week No. 22)

“At 2-1, they are getting some good play from Aaron Rodgers. He looked like the old Rodgers in the victory over the Bengals.” – Pete Prisco

Pro Football Talk: No.13 (Last Week No. 18)

“There’s some magic left in the post-Tomlin Steelers.” – Mike Florio

NFL.com: No.19 (Last Week No.26)

“Pittsburgh’s offense woke up! It was refreshing to watch the Steelers finally produce with the approach (aggressively pushing the ball downfield) they’ve been trying to force this season. It wasn’t at all surprising that their defense was the one to finish the job, either. I won’t be taken for an easy sale, though; they’ll need to do it more than once offensively for me to emotionally invest.” – Nick Shook

Yahoo! Sports: No.17 (Last Week No. 23)

Maybe the Steelers stumbled upon a solution for their offense: Turn Jaylen Warren into a workhorse. Last season, he played 47.4% of the Steelers’ snaps, a lower percentage than Kenneth Gainwell. In Week 1, with Rico Dowdle having been added over the offseason, Warren was at 37.3% of snaps. Dowdle was injured in Week 2, and in Week 3 Warren had the backfield to himself. He had 127 rushing yards on 17 carries and 49 receiving yards on three catches. That opened up the Steelers’ offense, which hadn’t played that well through two weeks. Aaron Rodgers had a strong game with 292 yards and three touchdowns. – Frank Schwab

USA Today: No.16 (Last Week No.27)

“An unanticipated offensive breakthrough vaulted them back to a 2-1 record and a four-way tie atop (at the bottom?) of the AFC North.” – Nate Davis

ESPN: No.17 (Last Week No. 25)

“None of Pittsburgh’s skill position players was projected to be a significant fantasy contributor, but Metcalf (WR31 in ADP) largely underperformed through the first three weeks with multiple drops, 11 catches and 98 receiving yards. Metcalf, though, might be turning a corner with the rest of the Steelers’ offense after finally recording a touchdown catch against the Bengals. He put up 12.1 fantasy points in the win.” – Brooke Pryor

The Steelers jumped up at least six spots, and as many as 11 spots in the rankings. Everyone is putting a lot of stock in just how good the offense looked against what looks to be a quality Bengals defense this season. Pittsburgh will have their work cut out for them on a short week as they travel to Cleveland to take on the Browns. The Steelers have not won a road game on Thursday Night Football since the 2007 season.

item.title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL, Week 3 Edition: All Hail Case Keenum
item.description: Check out @kdthompson5’s 10 Thoughts on the NFL: 49ers have an MVP candidate, the Packers stink, Super Bowl hangover, Case Keenum(!) and more
item.content:encoded:
1. If that Monday Night Football game was a “true team loss” for the Philadelphia Eagles, it was no less of a “true team win” for the Chicago Bears. Head coach Ben Johnson actually had ESPN color analyst Troy Aikman saying NFL teams would take what Case Keenum—a guy who is now on his eighth NFL team—did in that game over what they’re getting from their starting quarterbacks. Also, after a disgusting Week 1 performance, Dennis Allen’s defense has now held two straight opponents under 10 points. With no Caleb Williams there to generate magic on offense, it seemed like everyone earned their paychecks on Monday. (Except for Sam Roush. Come on, man.)

2. For some reason, the juxtaposition between two “go-for-it” decisions in that Monday night game felt especially poetic. Not surprisingly, Aikman spent nearly a half-quarter of action dogging Johnson’s decision to go for it on 4th-and-goal with the Bears up 7-0 rather than simply taking the points. Because there’s nothing more sacred to the older generation of former players than taking field goals over the risk of potentially failing to score a touchdown. Later, with the Eagles down by 13 and facing a 4th-and-1 from their own 49-yard line, Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni opted to punt and play field position with the Bears, a decision he expressed regret for after the game. One of these coaches was trying to win the game with a backup quarterback and was willing to take risks to do it. The other was more worried about not losing, or waiting for the other team to gift them an opportunity to win. The team that played to win created their own chances and won as a result. Maybe the old heads will get it eventually.

3. Not Kyle Shanahan busting out a hook-and-ladder in the first quarter to get a score against the Arizona Cardinals. So disrespectful, and yet so clean at the same time. Deebo Samuel Sr. might not have loved the way he was used all the time during his first stint by the Bay, but he’s got to admit no one works as hard to get him the ball as Shanahan does. Also…it’s not at all crazy to say the early MVP race is between Josh Allen and Brock Purdy, who currently has nine touchdowns versus just one pick and leads the league in passer rating.

4. I know it can’t erase the misery of last season’s ending, but seeing Baltimore Ravens kicker Tyler Loop hit that 56-yard game-winner in Rio this Sunday after blowing a kick to send Baltimore to the playoffs last season was a really cool bit of redemption. Football is a tough sport. It knocks you down a lot—both literally and figuratively. The ones who stick around in the game are the ones who keep getting up off the mat. Good on the kid. Just as cool: Lamar Jackson, who defended Loop after the aforementioned miss last year, looking (if possible) even more excited for his teammate hitting the kick than Loop did himself. That’s what being a real teammate and leader looks like.

5. We just can’t go a week without some controversial overturned call altering the outcome of a game, can we? This latest one went in the Denver Broncos’ favor when a Bo Nix interception late in the fourth quarter was undone by a questionable pass interference call that even rules analyst Terry McAulay hated. The most annoying part of the Broncos’ comeback win, though? We have to listen to more think pieces on how Nix, who is objectively mid, is somehow the best quarterback in a suddenly underwhelming 2024 class. As if Caleb Williams doesn’t exist.

6. The J.J. McCarthy trade to the Giants has made big headlines, especially with Jaxson Dart now lost for the season with a knee injury. But if we’re being completely real here, it’s not going to matter long-term. Dart is so much better than McCarthy that the idea of the latter usurping the starting role from the former feels ridiculous. Plus, if McCarthy couldn’t figure out how to get better with Kevin O’Connell, what makes you think Matt Nagy, the guy who made a healthy Patrick Mahomes look mortal the last few years, is magically going to help him figure it out? There’s a greater likelihood McCarthy isn’t on the Giants’ roster this time next year than that he’s their new QB1.

7. Good lord, the Green Bay Packers stink, and it’s a beautiful thing to behold. They can’t block anyone. They can’t tackle anyone. They just got smacked up and down the field by an Atlanta Falcons team that came into the game 0-2 and doesn’t have a quarterback, for all intents and purposes. I didn’t have Green Bay speed-running a trip to the bottom of the NFC North this early with a healthy Jordan Love, but I’m not going to turn up my nose at it.

8. Speaking of backups: Marcus Mariota did his thing against the defending champion Seattle Seahawks on Sunday, throwing for three scores and sealing the game with a patented run against one of the league’s best defenses. Look at Jameis Winston and Mariota still starting games 11 years after being the top two picks in the 2015 NFL Draft, respectively. Sure, it’s not for the teams that drafted them, and they haven’t been consistently starting-caliber guys for a while. But that’s what being a good locker room guy and a solid student can do for a guy. Mr. McCarthy, take notes. 

9. I’ve heard of Super Bowl hangovers. But it seems like the New England Patriots might need to get their collective stomachs pumped. Because this is beyond a simple sluggish start. In particular, Boston media is already on the verge of either discarding Drake Maye, the MVP runner-up from last season who has been dreadful so far (one TD, eight turnovers), moving on from head coach Mike Vrabel, or both. All those good vibes from just a few months ago? Yeah…those went out the window as soon as those vacation photos hit. 

10. This week’s question for the audience: whom do you want to see lose more on Thursday night—Aaron Rodgers or Deshaun Watson? I’m pretty clearly a bigger Watson hater in this case, but you’ll never catch me siding with Rodgers just because I’m hate-watching the other guy. Hopefully that game ends in a tie. It’s the closest we can get to them both losing.

item.title: Jaxon Smith-Njigba was interviewed by Russell Wilson, and he had a priceless quote
item.description: One Seahawks legend interviews a Seahawks legend in the making.
item.content:encoded:
Although legendary Seattle Seahawks quarterback Russell Wilson was traded one year before the franchise selected wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba in the 2023 NFL Draft, the superstar wideout is clearly still tapped in with some of the signal caller’s iconic NFL moments.

In his Sept. 29 appearance on CBS Sports’ Set, Hut!, hosted by Wilson and Kyle Long, Smith-Njigba was asked what it means to have quarterback Sam Darnold back after a two week absence—and he couldn’t help but sneak in one of Wilson’s viral taglines.

“For him to be out there, it felt right, it felt comfortable and we’re excited to build together but he’s our guy, we have ultimate trust in him—UNLIMITED trust,” he said while trying to contain laughter.

To no surprise, Wilson couldn’t help but have a good chuckle as well while thinking back to the moment. The iconic tagline stemmed from a 2018 video posted to Twitter from the all-time great quarterback where he talked about his alter ego, “Mr. Unlimited.”

Wilson accumulated 18,407 yards and 147 touchdowns to go alongside Pro Bowl selections in 2018-2021, while also being named a Second-Team All-Pro once across his final four seasons with the team after the viral video was released.

The “unlimited” title has been passed onto Darnold, so only time will tell if he’ll follow in Wilson’s footsteps.

item.title: Could the 49ers be a trade fit for former 1st round WR?
item.description: The Niners still need receiving help. Where should they go?
item.content:encoded:
Amidst their current injury situation, the San Francisco 49ers looked to bring in more bodies at wide receiver ahead of Week 4. Following a tryout, they signed former second-round pick Dante Pettis to the practice squad, making another change to a room that has seen a ton of movement so far.

The 49ers have dealt with injuries to Ricky Pearsall, De’Zhaun Stribling, Demarcus Robinson, Christian Kirk, and Mike Evans so far this season, forcing them to sign Khadarel Hodge, Brandin Cooks, and now Pettis to either their active roster or the practice squad.

It certainly isn’t an ideal situation for San Francisco, but the 49ers are 3-0 and humming on offense regardless. Pettis was one of nine players who worked out for the 49ers on Tuesday, and he comes to San Francisco after spending the 2025 season with the New Orleans Saints.

Pettis played eight games in 2025, catching nine passes for 127 yards. He’ll be a depth fill-in piece for the time being.

The 49ers are expected to have much of their receiver talent back at some point this season, set aside Pearsall, so making a major move at the position may not be their top priority. But there is an intriguing receiver candidate who could be had for cheap: former first-round pick Brian Thomas Jr.

Thomas, drafted by the Jacksonville Jaguars in the first round of the 2024 NFL Draft, has dealt with injury and inconsistency issues through his first three years. Through three games, he has just seven catches for 88 yards, while playing only 42 percent of the team’s offensive snaps, easily a career low.

Thomas had a down sophomore campaign in 2025, catching only 48 passes for 707 yards and two touchdowns, as he posted a catch rate under 53 percent. But he was excellent as a rookie, catching 87 passes for 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns, making the Pro Bowl.

With Thomas’s snaps continuing to dwindle, he could be a trade candidate for the Jaguars, who reportedly listened to offers this offseason. And the 49ers could be a top fit, given their need for receiver talent and desire to stay on the younger side.

The 49ers have needed that field-stretcher with their injuries. That role initially went to Ricky Pearsall, then De’Zhaun Stribling, then Demarcus Robinson, and now Khadarel Hodge. Having some consistency there by trading for Thomas could be a short-term, and maybe even long-term, solution.

The cost to acquire the Jaguars receiver shouldn’t be too high at the moment, given his role is dwindling, but Thomas seems more and more likely to be dealt and fits what the 49ers want as a cost-controlled receiver who can play the role of their injured receivers.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers ties Ben Roethlisberger with 165 career wins, fifth-most ever
item.description: By beating the Bengals on Sunday, Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers equaled former Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger's career win total.
item.content:encoded:
By beating the Bengals on Sunday, Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers equaled former Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger's career win total.

Both Rodgers and Roethlisberger have exactly 165 regular-season wins as a starting quarterback, tied for the fifth-most ever. Roethlisberger played his entire career with the Steelers, while Rodgers has 147 wins with the Packers, 12 with the Steelers and six with the Jets.

The all-time record for wins by a starting quarterback may never be broken: Tom Brady retired with 251 career wins, 219 with the Patriots and 32 with the Buccaneers. You could take Rodgers' stellar career, add five 17-0 seasons on top of it, and you'd still be one win short of Brady's career win total.

Tied for second place in all-time wins are Brett Favre and Peyton Manning, each with 186. Favre won 160 starts with the Packers, 17 with the Vikings and nine with the Jets. Manning won 141 starts with the Colts and 45 with the Broncos.

Rodgers has a chance to surpass No. 4 on the all-time wins list, Drew Brees, who won 172 career games: 142 with the Saints and 30 with the Chargers. If Rodgers and the Steelers win eight more games this season, Rodgers will retire ahead of Brees and behind only Brady, Manning and Favre on the all-time wins list.

item.title: Los Angeles Chargers news: Panic meter reaches new high with Justin Herbert
item.description: The panic meter is hitting a new high with Justin Herbert after his latest outing against the Bills.
item.content:encoded:
It’s not just the Chargers fan base that’s starting to freak out about Justin Herbert and the Chargers offense.

ESPN insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano got together to discuss the latest around the NFL and part of that was discussing the panic meter for several underperforming quarterbacks. Of course, Justin Herbert was among that small group that included Cam Ward and Drake Maye.

With more picks than touchdown passes through three games, Herbert’s too easy of a selection not to be discussed.

“Jumping to Herbert, his play is inexcusably bad, but he’s in Year 7 with 98 career starts, with most of those played at a high level,” says Fowler. ‘‘He has proof of concept more so than Maye or Ward. The jumbled offense under offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel hasn’t helped. And I’m not exactly sure where they turn next.”

Graziano’s opinion unfortunately did not differ much from Fowler.

“Yikes. Talk about disconnect between player and scheme. Everything looks “difficult and exhausting” for Herbert, using the words of one evaluator I spoke to last week. There was so much talk in the offseason about how Herbert and his immense natural talent would flourish under McDaniel, but it’s clearly not clicking. A fresh wave of offensive line injuries that happened as the season was getting underway certainly didn’t help. But the run game can’t get going, the receivers haven’t taken the jumps we were promised, and Herbert has looked confused and overwhelmed by whatever it is he’s being asked to do out there.”

“A lot of people have theories on what the Chargers need to do in terms of simplifying things so they can just start having success to build on. But there’s also concern that the personnel doesn’t fit what the offense is built to do, which might be difficult to overcome.”

Despite it all, Fowler believes the old Herbert is still in there somewhere.

‘‘Look, Herbert has excelled as a true pocket passer, whereas McDaniel thrived having Tua Tagovailoa throw with anticipation to spots. Either Herbert struggles to do both or McDaniel isn’t putting him in a position to show that he can. I still think Herbert has good football in him, but that’s harder to sell by the week. And your point about mismatched personnel is a good one.”

item.title: Packers sign Wisconsin native Kevin Zeitler in latest OL move
item.description: The former Badger and Wisconsin native is coming out of retirement and returning home.
item.content:encoded:
A prodigal son is coming home. Kevin Zeitler, a 14-year veteran and Pro Bowl right guard, is returning back to the state of Wisconsin to sign with the Green Bay Packers.

ESPN’s Adam Schefter reports that the Packers are signing Zeitler on Wednesday, one day after he worked out for the team. Zeitler, who comes out of unofficial retirement with the signing, becomes the third veteran guard and second former Pro Bowler to sign with the Packers since the team’s Week 3 loss last Thursday night, joining Laken Tomlinson (signed to the 53-man roster) and Mekhi Becton (practice squad).

Zeitler, a Waukesha native, played for the Wisconsin Badgers during some of their finest seasons in recent memory, serving as the team’s starting right guard from 2009 to 2011. The Badgers won double-digit games in each of those three years and made two Rose Bowl appearances, while Zeitler earned first-team All-American honors as a senior in 2011. He then became a first-round draft pick in 2012, selected 27th overall by the Cincinnati Bengals.

In his 14 NFL seasons, Zeitler has played for six different teams, but has remained a quality, steady player at every single stop. Most recently, he started 16 games for the Tennessee Titans in 2025 while on a one-year, $9 million contract. Unlike Tomlinson and Becton, Zeitler likely will draw a significant salary for the remainder of the season.

The move was telegraphed a bit by Becton changing his jersey number almost immediately after signing earlier in the week:

Zeitler’s lone Pro Bowl appearance came at age 33, earning the honor for the 2023 season as a member of the Baltimore Ravens. He then signed a one-year, $6 million deal with the Detroit Lions for 2024, making 16 starts, before landing in Tennessee a year ago.

This is easily the highest-profile and most significant of the three signings this week, however. Once up to speed with the Packers’ offense, Zeitler should be an immediate upgrade over Jacob Monk at right guard while the Packers continue working to sort out the left guard position with a battle between the likes of Tomlinson, Aaron Banks, and others.

UPDATE: Zeitler’s contract is for a surprisingly low amount of money, given rumors that had put him at between $6-8 million. According to Ian Rapoport, the deal is only a one-year, $4.05 million contract with incentives that could take it to a maximum of $5 million.
